Guard checked: internal/central/adapter/deferred_creation_live_toggle_test.go:44-52 builds `m.byCentral` by hand with a single `cbHandlers: h`. It cannot observe a second handler instance, so it covers the XML-RPC path only — as the candidate suspected.
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false, either `centralBringUp` would carry more than one handler (a slice/map) or `wireCUxDInterface` would hand its instance back to the manager — a second assignment to `h.cbHandlers`, or a `Register/Attach*Handlers` call reachable from cuxd_wiring.go. The `cbHandlers` grep over internal/ and cmd/ returns one struct field (central_bringup.go:36), one assignment (central_bringup.go:396) and one unrelated function-local in cuxd_wiring.go:173. That is the result the false case would not have produced.
stands.reason: Two live CallbackHandlers instances per central carry the same operator decision; only the XML-RPC one is reachable from ApplyDeferredCreationBehavior. Severity medium rather than high because the already-held devices ARE freed for CUxD too: releaseEveryHeldDevice (central_bringup.go:328-347) walks `u.ModelRegistry.List()` and calls `u.Devices.ReleaseAllParked(ctx)` per unit, not per interface. What stays broken is every subsequent CUxD announcement, in both directions.
stands.divergence: Runtime toggle flip on a central that has CUxD wired. OFF→ON: ApplyDeferredCreationBehavior sets the XML-RPC handler's flag to true; the BIN-RPC handler registered at cuxd_wiring.go:180 still holds false, so the next CUxD `newDevices` callback takes the `h.goBackground(...)` immediate-ingest branch (callback_handlers.go:579) and creates entities the operator just asked to hold. ON→OFF: the CUxD handler still holds true, so the next CUxD `newDevices` takes the `StoreDelayedDeviceDescriptions` branch (callback_handlers.go:569) and parks the device although the toggle is off. Same input, two answers, decided by which transport announced the device.
stands.deadCopy: Neither copy is dead. Both handler instances are registered on live callback servers (deps.CallbackServer.Register(cc.Name, handlers) at ccu_wiring.go:645; binrpcCallbackServer.Register(initID, handlers) at cuxd_wiring.go:180). The CUxD copy is unreachable from the manager, not unreachable from the wire.
stands.guard: internal/central/adapter/deferred_creation_live_toggle_test.go — TestTurningTheToggleOffAppliesWithoutARestart; covers the XML-RPC handler only (hand-built byCentral with one cbHandlers at :50). No guard covers the BIN-RPC handler.
stands.secondReason: Survived every attack. Quotes are verbatim and current; both handler instances are constructed in production wiring and both are reachable from a live callback server (XML-RPC by central name, BIN-RPC by interface id); the toggle path is a hot-reload that changes only the XML-RPC instance and never re-wires the central. The divergence is reproducible by reading the one shared branch: CallbackHandlers.NewDevices at callback_handlers.go:560 (`if h.delayNewDeviceCreation.Load() {`) parks into StoreDelayedDeviceDescriptions at :569 or ingests immediately via `h.goBackground(...)` at :579 — and after a runtime flip the two instances answer that branch differently, decided only by which transport announced the device. Severity medium is right, not high: the OFF direction's already-held devices ARE freed for CUxD too, because releaseEveryHeldDevice (central_bringup.go:328-347) walks `u.ModelRegistry.List()` and calls `u.Devices.ReleaseAllParked(ctx)` per unit, not per interface. What stays broken is every later CUxD announcement in both directions. Note the finding's own cuxd_wiring.go:179/180 line cites are exact.

stands.title: The activation retry loop and its client-state walk are implemented twice
stands.evidence:
Quotes verified, and I diffed the two bodies rather than eyeballing them: ccu_wiring.go:1402-1431 against cuxd_wiring.go:388-417 differ only in the four-line vs three-line comment above the exhaustion branch. Every statement is identical, including `for attempt := 0; ; attempt++ {`, `err := activate(ingestAttemptContext(ctx, attempt, len(backoff)))`, `if err == nil { return true }`, `if attempt >= len(backoff) { … ensureDisconnectedClientState(ic, err, logger); return false }`, the Debug retry log, and `select { case <-ctx.Done(): t.Stop(); ensureDisconnectedClientState(ic, ctx.Err(), logger); return false; case <-t.C: } }`.

The load-bearing rule is documented at ccu_wiring.go:1386-1393: `// The DISCONNECTED walk is the load-bearing half: activate() fails inside` / `// IngestFromBackend, well before the init()/callback block …` / `// CanReconnect is false in CREATED, so the recovery pipeline rejected every` / `// trigger with "CanReconnect returned false" and the interface served zero` / `// devices until a daemon restart.`

Both live: ccu_wiring.go:1343 and cuxd_wiring.go:277.

Guards: each copy has its own suite — ccu_wiring_activation_test.go:55/:88/:115 and cuxd_wiring_test.go:32/:69/:102 — covering retry-success, exhaustion and ctx-cancel. Nothing compares the two.
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false, one function would delegate to the other (a shared helper called from both files), and the diff of the two 30-line windows would not have come back as comment-text-only. Had the CUxD side's guards been symmetric with the XML-RPC side's, cuxd_wiring_test.go:102 would have passed a real *client.InterfaceClient and asserted its state; it passes `nil` and asserts only `calls` and `ingested`.
stands.reason: Two byte-identical live implementations of a rule whose own doc records the defect it exists to fix. The concrete asymmetry is in the guards, not the code: internal/central/adapter/ccu_wiring_activation_test.go:113-131 (TestRunXMLRPCActivationStopsOnContextCancel) builds a real client via newActivationTestClient(t) and asserts `if got := ic.ClientState(); got != hmenum.ClientStateDisconnected { … }`, while internal/central/adapter/cuxd_wiring_test.go:89-115 (TestRunCUxDActivationStopsOnContextCancel) passes `nil, "ccu", "ccu-CUxD", discardLogger()` for the client and asserts nothing about client state. Deleting `ensureDisconnectedClientState(ic, ctx.Err(), logger)` from cuxd_wiring.go:413 leaves the whole suite green; deleting it from ccu_wiring.go:1428 turns one test red. Medium: a CUxD interface left in CREATED after a cancelled boot ingest has CanReconnect false and serves zero devices until a restart, which is exactly the defect ccu_wiring.go:1386-1393 documents.
stands.divergence: No runtime divergence today — the two bodies are identical. The divergence that exists today is in coverage: the ctx-cancel branch's DISCONNECTED walk is pinned on the XML-RPC copy (ccu_wiring_activation_test.go:129 asserts ClientStateDisconnected) and unpinned on the CUxD copy (cuxd_wiring_test.go:104 passes a nil *client.InterfaceClient). stands.title: "Does this description carry marker M" is HasPrefix in markerMatch and Contains in parseSysvarDescription — same rawDesc, contradictory answers
stands.evidence:
Quotes verified verbatim. hub_wiring.go:890-901: `func markerMatch(desc string, markers []hmenum.DescriptionMarker) bool { if len(markers) == 0 { return true } / d := strings.TrimSpace(desc) / for _, m := range markers { if m != "" && strings.HasPrefix(d, string(m)) { return true } } / return false }`. hub_wiring.go:1114-1131: `func parseSysvarDescription(raw string) (cleaned string, isExtended bool) { … for _, m := range markers { if strings.Contains(out, string(m)) { if m == sysvarDescriptionMarker { isExtended = true } / out = strings.ReplaceAll(out, string(m), "") } } }`.

BOTH RUN ON THE SAME STRING, in the same function body: internal/central/adapter/hub_wiring.go:1243 `desc, isExtended := parseSysvarDescription(rawDesc)` and :1271 `EnabledDefault: hubEnabledDefault(v.IsInternal, rawDesc, opts.sysvarMarkers),` — hubEnabledDefault delegates to markerMatch at :940 `return markerMatch(desc, markers)`. rawDesc is the decoded ReGa DPInfo text (hub_wiring.go:1195-1198).

Both sides are LIVE: upsertSysvar is called from the production loadSysvars loop (hub_wiring.go:1203); markerMatch is additionally reached for programs via hubEnabledDefault at hub_wiring.go:1056 and :1062. Marker tokens are `HAHM`/`HX`/`INTERNAL`/`MQTT` (pkg/hmenum/device.go:114-117) — uppercase, not the lowercase `hahm` the candidate's prose used; the defect is unaffected.

Cross-check against the reference stack whose contract markerMatch's own comment claims to mirror ("It mirrors the reference stack", hub_wiring.go:903-908): the reference matches markers by SUBSTRING, not prefix. ../aiohomematic/aiohomematic/client/json_rpc.py:2459-2464 calls `element_matches_key(search_elements=markers, compare_with=description, ignore_case=False, do_left_wildcard_search=True)`, and with both wildcards on that reduces to `if element in compare_with_processed: return True` (../aiohomematic/aiohomematic/support/__init__.py:385-387). Its own fixture is `{"ext1": "#HAHM# External"}` with the comment `# ext1 matches the HAHM marker via description` (../aiohomematic/tests/test_client_json_rpc_client.py:2081-2090) — a description in which the marker is deliberately NOT a prefix. So the prefix half is the divergent one, against both its sibling and the contract it cites.
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false I would have seen one of two things at the cited lines: markerMatch using Contains/a regex like parseSysvarDescription (identical predicates, no divergence), or the two functions fed different strings — e.g. hubEnabledDefault called with the already-cleaned `desc` rather than `rawDesc`, which would make the comparison meaningless. I read hub_wiring.go:1243 and :1271 in the same function body and both take `rawDesc`; and I read the two predicates and they are HasPrefix vs Contains.
stands.reason: One question — does this sysvar's description carry marker token M — answered by two live predicates on the same input, with a concrete input on which they already disagree, and the prefix half contradicts the reference contract its own doc comment invokes. Severity medium and not high because the disagreement needs a non-prefixed marker: the operator-visible effect is confined to that description shape, and it degrades (extended shape, disabled by default) rather than corrupting data.
stands.divergence: rawDesc = "Heizung HAHM", cfg sysvar_markers = [HAHM], v.IsInternal = false. parseSysvarDescription("Heizung HAHM") → isExtended = TRUE, cleaned = "Heizung" (Contains hits). hubEnabledDefault(false, "Heizung HAHM", [HAHM]) → markerMatch → strings.HasPrefix("Heizung HAHM", "HAHM") = false → EnabledDefault = FALSE. Same sysvar, same string: created in its extended (writable switch/select/number) shape and simultaneously left disabled by default. The mirror input "HAHM Heizung" makes both true, which is why the common case hides it.
stands.guard: None ties the two. TestMarkerMatch (internal/central/adapter/hub_scan_toggles_test.go:221) pins the prefix half explicitly and deliberately — its table contains `{"kitchen HAHM", []hmenum.DescriptionMarker{hmenum.DescriptionMarkerHAHM}, false}, // not a prefix` — so it would stay green while parseSysvarDescription says the opposite. TestHubEnabledDefault (same file:198) uses only prefixed descriptions ("HAHM x"). No test feeds one description to both functions.
stands.deadCopy: Neither. Both have production callers: parseSysvarDescription at hub_wiring.go:1243, markerMatch via hubEnabledDefault at hub_wiring.go:940 from :1271 (sysvars) and :1056/:1062 (programs).
stands.secondReason: Survives every bite. The quotes are verbatim and current; both predicates are live and, uniquely, run on the *same variable in the same function body*; the diverging input is reproducible and reachable. On rawDesc="Heizung HAHM" with sysvar_markers=[HAHM] and IsInternal=false: parseSysvarDescription returns isExtended=true (Contains hits), so ApplyMeta stamps IsExtended=true and sysvar_subtypes.go gives the writable switch/select/number shape; hubEnabledDefault falls through to markerMatch, HasPrefix("Heizung HAHM","HAHM")=false, so EnabledDefault=false. One sysvar, one string, two opposite answers to "does this carry HAHM". I attacked the sameness hardest, since a stripper legitimately needs Contains — but the split does not survive it: isExtended is not a by-product of stripping, it is a separate boolean answering the marker question, and the reference implements *both* halves with the same substring predicate (json_rpc.py:2458 and :2489), so they never disagree there. Nor is the input filtered upstream, and it is not exotic: because the reference matches substrings, an operator migrating from that stack can legitimately have written the marker anywhere in the description. Two further things I did not expect and that strengthen rather than weaken it: the operator help text at i18n.ts:1782 promises a single verb — the description "may carry" the token — for both consequences it then describes separately (enabled, and writable), which is exactly the promise the prefix half breaks; and the prefix semantics diverge from the reference contract with no entry in notes/parity/by_design.md (grep for marker there returns only unrelated items at :194, :500, :721, :2043, :3961). The only thing arguing against acting is hub_scan_toggles_test.go:233, which pins "kitchen HAHM" → false as deliberate — but a test pinning the current behaviour is not a justification for it, and the comment `// not a prefix` records the mechanism, not a reason. Severity stays medium and not high, for the reason the finding gives: the effect is confined to non-prefixed descriptions and degrades (extended shape, disabled by default, operator can switch it on) rather than corrupting data or reaching a CCU write. The sharpest statement of the defect is not "a duplicated rule" but "markerMatch answers a substring question with a prefix test"; parseSysvarDescription's Contains is the correct half.

stands.title: Two independent climate weekday -> 13-slot expanders that disagree on overflow
stands.evidence: Both quotes verified verbatim. internal/central/adapter/schedules.go:1558-1561: `if len(stretches) > schedule.MaxClimateSlots {` / `return nil, fmt.Errorf("too many periods: yielded %d slots, max %d",` / `len(stretches), schedule.MaxClimateSlots)` / `}`. internal/model/weekprofile/slot.go:122-127: `out := make(weekdaySlots, slotCount)` / `for no, s := range ws {` / `if no >= 1 && no <= slotCount {` / `out[no] = s` / `}` / `}` — reached from internal/model/weekprofile/rawconvert.go:410 `return fillUpWeekdaySlots(cwd.BaseTemperature, ws), nil`. internal/model/schedule/climate.go:43-46 verified verbatim: `It is an UPPER bound on a smaller quantity: a period preceded by a gap expands to two slots, so a day validated by [ClimateWeekday.ValidateWire] (which does not enforce gapless coverage) can still exceed the slot count.` Liveness: adapter side live (internal/north/rest/handlers/schedules.go:143 -> schedule_query_adapter.go:58 -> SchedulesDomain.PutClimateSchedule -> schedules.go:1034 serializeClimateSchedule -> expandWeekday). Model side: repo-wide grep for `SetWeekday`, `CopyScheduleTo`, `CopyProfileTo`, `SetSchedule(`, `SetProfile(` and `.Save(` returns NO non-_test.go caller — SchedulesDomain.SetSchedule is called only from schedule_io.go:245 (SetWeekday) and :387 (CopyScheduleTo), both themselves callerless; the DP-bound climateChannelSaver (week_profile_io.go:71) is installed at week_profile_filter.go:461 but weekprofile.Profile.Save is only reached from CopyClimateProfileKey/CopyClimateSchedule (profile.go:264/290) and combined.WeekProfile.Set (weekprofile.go:189), none of which has a production caller.
stands.negativeControl: Had the two expanders agreed, expandWeekday would carry the same silent trim-and-pad as fillUpWeekdaySlots (or fillUpWeekdaySlots an error return); instead schedules.go:1558 returns an error on the exact input where slot.go:124's bound check drops the entry. Had the model chain been live, the grep for callers of SetSchedule / SetWeekday / CopyScheduleTo / CopyProfileTo / Profile.Save outside _test.go would have produced at least one hit — it produced none.
stands.divergence: BaseTemperature 17.0 with seven gapped periods at 22.0: 01:00-02:00, 03:00-04:00, 05:00-06:00, 07:00-08:00, 09:00-10:00, 11:00-12:00, 13:00-14:00. One payload, three answers. (a) adapter expandWeekday: 7 gap-fills + 7 periods + trailing fill = 15 stretches -> error `too many periods: yielded 15 slots, max 13`, REST PUT refused. (b) model climateWeekdayToSlotsWire: ValidateWire passes (7 <= 13 periods, no overlap), climateWeekdayToSlotsExpand builds ws[1..15], fillUpWeekdaySlots keeps only 1..13 -> the written day ends at slot 13 = ENDTIME 13:00 / base 17.0; the 13:00-14:00 22.0 window and the 24:00 terminator are both dropped, so the device holds a day that stops at 13:00. (c) model climateWeekdayToSlots (strict): rejected by ClimateWeekday.Validate with `schedule: first period must start at 00:00 (got 01:00)` — a third answer to the same payload.
stands.deadCopy: Model side. weekprofile.ClimateToRaw / ClimateToRawWire / BuildClimateRawParamset reach PutParamset only through SchedulesDomain.SetSchedule/SetProfile/CopyProfileTo and climateChannelSaver.Save; none of those has a caller outside _test.go. The adapter's expandWeekday is the only climate expander a running daemon executes.
stands.guard: None couples the two. tests/contract/weekprofile_slots_slot_limit_test.go (TestWeekprofileSlotsEncoderCarriesEverythingTheValidatorAdmits) drives only the model side, and only with a gapless day built by weekprofileSlotsGaplessDay — a shape where periods == slots, so the overflow branch is never reached and expandWeekday is never called. internal/central/adapter/schedule_slot_limit_test.go pins the two climate READ paths, not the write encoders.
stands.reason: The duplication and the overflow disagreement are real and I reproduced the diverging input by reading both bodies. Two parts of the candidate's damage claim are refuted: (1) `both are write paths onto the same MASTER paramset` — only the adapter's is; the model's whole climate write chain is test-only, so no operator can currently be handed a truncated day. (2) `the two REST entry points give opposite answers for the same payload` — there is one REST entry point for climate writes (PUT /devices/{addr}/channels/{no}/schedule -> PutClimateSchedule), and it uses the adapter expander. Severity dropped from high to medium: nothing breaks today, but the model half is a fully-built, test-green API whose first production wiring ships silent truncation, and no guard would notice.
stands.secondReason: The duplication and the overflow disagreement survive: two independent expanders, one erroring and one truncating, with no shared implementation and no guard covering the gapped over-13 case (tests/contract/weekprofile_slots_slot_limit_test.go pins only the gapless day, where one period maps to one slot). What does not survive is the damage narrative, and that is why I drop severity to low. The claim 'the model half is a fully-built API whose first production wiring ships silent truncation' is refuted in both directions the model actually offers. (a) The operator-shaped API (SetSchedule/SetProfile/SetWeekday) goes through ClimateToRaw -> climateWeekdayToSlots -> ClimateWeekday.Validate, which enforces gapless 00:00-24:00 coverage (climate.go:100-114) and <=13 periods; a gapless day emits no gap-fill and no trailing fill, so stretches == len(periods) <= 13 and truncation is unreachable by construction. (b) The wire-form API (CopyProfileTo, climateChannelSaver) is documented to take authoritative CCU data (rawconvert.go:263 'use ClimateToRawWire for [CopyProfileTo] where the source is authoritative CCU data'), and that data cannot re-expand above 13: slotsToClimateWeekday (rawconvert.go:418-482) merges only ADJACENT equal-temperature slots and drops base-valued stretches, so re-expansion reconstructs at most the original partition — a <=13-slot CCU day round-trips to <=13 stretches. Truncation therefore requires a future caller feeding synthetic gapped data to the wire path, not merely wiring the existing API. Also worth recording against 'no guard would notice': internal/model/schedule/climate.go:41-46 already names this exact gap in prose ('a period preceded by a gap expands to two slots, so a day validated by [ClimateWeekday.ValidateWire] ... can still exceed the slot count'), so it is an acknowledged limitation, not an unnoticed drift. Net: a real, unguarded duplication of one firmware rule with two different overflow contracts — worth de-duplicating, not worth a medium.

stands.title: The CCU 'Dauerhaft' pair (7, 31) is spelled in three places, one of them as a bare literal
stands.evidence: All three quotes verified verbatim. internal/model/weekprofile/rawconvert.go:1096-1099: `const (` / `permanentBase   = 7 // HOUR_1` / `permanentFactor = 31` / `)`, preceded at :1056-1095 by the firmware citation (`www/config/easymodes/js/HmIPWeeklyProgram.js`, `if (parseInt(value) == 0) { factorElm.val(31); baseElm.val(7); }`). internal/central/adapter/schedules.go:684-687: `const (` / `lockPermissionDurationBase   = 7  // HOUR_1` / `lockPermissionDurationFactor = 31 // -> sentinel "always"` / `)`. internal/model/schedule/lock.go:29-33: `var LockActionTable = map[LockAction]LockActionRaw{` / `LockActionAutoRelockStart: {level: 0.0, durBase: 0, durFactor: 0},` / `LockActionAutoRelockEnd:   {level: 0.0, durBase: 7, durFactor: 31},` / `LockActionUnlock:          {level: 1.0, durBase: 7, durFactor: 31},` / `LockActionOpen:            {level: 1.01, durBase: 7, durFactor: 31},`. All three live: rawconvert.go:757 (decodeWireDuration), :1222 and :1250-1251 (ParseTimeBaseFactor) are on the live read/encode path; schedules.go:929 `e.Duration = weekprofile.FormatTimeBaseFactor(lockPermissionDurationBase, lockPermissionDurationFactor)` runs inside applyLockEncoding, reached from serializeSimpleScheduleWithDomain (schedules.go:897-902) on the live PUT path; LockActionTable is read by DetectLockAction / EncodeLockAction, bridged at schedules.go:681 and used at :911.
stands.negativeControl: Had one site already drifted, its pair would not read (7, 31) — I opened all three and every one spells base 7 / factor 31. Had a guard coupled them, a test would reference lockPermissionDurationBase; grep across all _test.go files finds that identifier nowhere.
stands.divergence: No numeric divergence, but a live representational one that follows from the split: the adapter reaches the pair as raw integers and formats it with weekprofile.FormatTimeBaseFactor, which does NOT special-case the permanent pair (rawconvert.go:1186-1199 walks timeBaseTable; row {7, "h", 1, 36000} at :1126). So a user_permission slot written through the SPA carries Duration `"31h"` on the DTO, while the same wire pair read back through decodeWireDuration (rawconvert.go:757) yields `"permanent"` (PermanentDuration, rawconvert.go:1171). The two strings still land on the same wire pair today only because ParseTimeBaseFactor carries an explicit escape hatch at :1246-1253 for exactly this value.
stands.deadCopy: Neither — all three sites have production callers.
stands.guard: None crossing packages. internal/model/weekprofile/permanent_duration_test.go pins the pair inside weekprofile only (it uses the unexported permanentBase/permanentFactor, so it cannot see the adapter's copy); internal/central/adapter/schedules_test.go:833-837 asserts the read path yields weekprofile.PermanentDuration but never touches lockPermissionDurationBase/Factor. Nothing asserts LockActionTable's durBase/durFactor against weekprofile's pair either.
stands.reason: Confirmed as stated: one firmware fact, three spellings, two of them bare literals with no citation, and no guard. The candidate's drift scenario is sound — rawconvert.go:1089-1091 names the observation that would move the encoding (`a device declaring DURATION_FACTOR MAX above 31`), and a fix applied there alone leaves schedules.go:685-686 and lock.go:31-33 writing the old pair, turning a standing lock permission into a timed one. Severity kept at medium: all three sites are live, but a change here is a deliberate edit rather than an accident waiting to fire.
stands.secondReason: Survives on quote, sameness and liveness: one firmware fact, three spellings, two of them uncited bare literals, all three on live paths, with no guard tying them. What does not survive is the specific damage narrative, which is why I drop severity to low. The candidate says a fix applied only at rawconvert.go would leave the other two 'writing the old pair, turning a standing lock permission into a timed one'. Traced, that direction fails loudly, not silently: applyLockEncoding hands FormatTimeBaseFactor(7,31) = '31h' straight back into ParseTimeBaseFactor on the way to the paramset, and if permanentFactor moved off 31 the escape hatch at rawconvert.go:1247-1252 would no longer match — 31h is 1,116,000 100ms steps, and every row of timeBaseTable divides it into a factor above MaxTimeBaseFactor=30 (3600s->31, 600s->186, 300s->372, 60s->1860, 10s->11160, 5s->22320, 1s->111600, 0.1s->1116000), so ParseTimeBaseFactor returns ok=false and the save fails with the 'invalid duration' error that internal/central/adapter/schedules_test.go:771-774 documents by name. Existing round-trip tests (TestParseTimeBaseFactorPermanentSentinel, TestTimeBaseFactorRoundTripPermanent, TestSerializeSimpleScheduleLockAutorelockEnd) would go red on that partial edit. A silent wrong write needs the opposite partial edit — changing LockActionTable's rows while leaving the weekprofile pair — which is a deliberate, narrower mistake. So: genuine triplication of one cited firmware constant, de-duplicable today by exporting the weekprofile pair or routing both call sites through ParseTimeBaseFactor(PermanentDuration), but the blast radius named in the finding is overstated.

stands.title: Duration strings have two grammars: the validator rejects what the encoder accepts and produces
stands.evidence: Both quotes verified verbatim at the cited lines. simple.go:159 durationPattern = regexp.MustCompile with the pattern ^\d+(?:ms|s|min|h)$ ; simple.go:172 'if err != nil || factor < 1 || factor > maxDurationFactor {' with 'const maxDurationFactor = 30' at simple.go:154. rawconvert.go:756-759 'func decodeWireDuration(base, factor int) string {' / 'if base == permanentBase && factor == permanentFactor {' / 'return PermanentDuration', with 'const PermanentDuration = "permanent"' at rawconvert.go:1171 and permanentBase=7 / permanentFactor=31 at rawconvert.go:1097-1098. rawconvert.go:1186-1198 FormatTimeBaseFactor returns ZeroDuration for factor 0 and otherwise fmt.Sprintf("%d%s", factor*row.mult, row.unit); 'const ZeroDuration = "0ms"' at rawconvert.go:1150. rawconvert.go:1221 'if strings.EqualFold(strings.TrimSpace(d), PermanentDuration) {'. The divergence is documented by the code itself at rawconvert.go:595-602: 'Validating here discarded real data: [schedule.SimpleEntry.Validate] caps a duration numeral at 30, which every slot on a coarse time base exceeds, so a switching programme with a 12-minute duration and every lock slot the CCU encodes with the "permanent" sentinel vanished from the surface instead of being displayed.'
stands.divergence: Three exact inputs. The doc claim at converter.go:14-16 is also verbatim and true for the encode direction: parameter.ConvertHMLevelToCPV is called from internal/model/custom/cover/blind.go:346 and tests/contract/level_combined_encoding_test.go:113. LIVENESS: the backends copy is live — internal/central/adapter/callback_handlers.go:293 `if backends.IsCombinedParameter(parameter)` and :434 `parsed, parsedOK := backends.ParseCombinedParameter(parameter, raw)`, plus internal/client/reliability/command_tracker.go:127 `values, ok := backends.ParseCombinedParameter(parameter, value)`. A repo-wide grep for `ConvertCPVToHMLevel|ConvertCPVToHMIPLevel` returns ONLY internal/model/value/converter.go (the definitions + its own doc comment) and internal/model/value/converter_test.go:125 / converter_extra_test.go:112 — no production caller anywhere. Guard: tests/contract/level_combined_encoding_test.go:144 exercises backends.ParseCombinedParameter only; internal/model/value/converter_test.go:113 exercises the model copy in isolation. No test compares the two.
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false I would have seen one of three things: (a) the cited lines not holding that code; (b) `grep -rn ConvertCPVToHMLevel --include=*.go .` returning a non-_test.go caller, which would have made this a live-vs-live divergence rather than a dead copy; or (c) the two implementations agreeing on every string input, which would have made the duplication cosmetic. All three checks were run and each returned the opposite: quotes match, zero non-test callers, and a concrete diverging input exists.
stands.reason: Two independent implementations of the same rule (raw/200), reached by different parsers, with the /100/2 constant written twice and nothing pinning them together. The finding is stronger than the bundle framed it, not weaker: the model/value copy is dead in production, so internal/model/value/converter_test.go:113 is a green test measuring a function no running daemon calls, while every real callback decode goes through the backends copy with its different (and differently-failing) parser. Severity is medium rather than high because there is no second live consumer today, so the two cannot disagree at runtime — the damage is a duplicated constant plus false test assurance, not a wrong cover position on the wire.
stands.divergence: Input "100" (a decimal LEVEL_COMBINED byte with no 0x prefix). backends.convertCpvLevelHm("100") takes the `!strings.HasPrefix(v, "0x")` branch at combined.go:160 and returns the STRING "100" (typed `any`), so the caller gets a string where a float64 is expected. value.ConvertCPVToHMLevel("100") returns (0.5, true) — a float64. Second diverging input: "010". Go's fmt scan with verb 'v' into an *int routes through scanBasePrefix (GOROOT/src/fmt/scan.go), whose `default:` arm after accepting a leading "0" selects octalDigits, so value.ConvertCPVToHMLevel("010") = 8/200 = 0.04, while backends returns the string "010". They agree only on the 0x/0X-prefixed form (scanBasePrefix's `case s.peek("xX")` selects base 16), which is the one shape both were written for.
stands.deadCopy: internal/model/value/converter.go:111 ConvertCPVToHMLevel and :123 ConvertCPVToHMIPLevel — no production caller; referenced only from internal/model/value/converter_test.go:125 and internal/model/value/converter_extra_test.go:112.
stands.guard: none comparing the two. tests/contract/level_combined_encoding_test.go pins the ENCODE direction (blind write path vs parameter.ConvertHMLevelToCPV) and round-trips only through backends.ParseCombinedParameter (:144); it never touches value.ConvertCPVToHMLevel.

The quote is exact, the line numbers are current, the deadness of the model/value copy is established by an exhaustive identifier grep (only its own unit test calls it), and the divergence is reproduced from the Go standard library source rather than from a convention about how %v parses. The type system does not force the repetition: internal/parameter already hosts the encode half and is importable from both packages, and internal/client/backends/ccu_extended.go:813 shows the codebase reaching a shared implementation through a narrow assertion when it wants to. The finding's own severity discount is right — the two cannot disagree at runtime today because only one is reachable — so the damage is a twice-written constant plus a green test that measures a function no running daemon calls. That is a backlog entry, not an incident.

stands.title: The convertable-parameter set {COMBINED_PARAMETER, LEVEL_COMBINED} is declared three times; the existing guard covers only two of the three
stands.evidence: All three quotes verified verbatim. internal/client/backends/combined.go:26-27: `parameterCombined      = "COMBINED_PARAMETER"` / `parameterLevelCombined = "LEVEL_COMBINED"`, consumed at :42 `return name == parameterCombined || name == parameterLevelCombined`. internal/parameter/converter.go:19-22: `var ConvertableParameters = map[hmenum.Parameter]struct{}{ hmenum.ParameterCombinedParameter: {}, hmenum.ParameterLevelCombined: {} }`. internal/model/value/converter.go:33-36: `var ConvertableParameters = [...]hmenum.Parameter{ hmenum.ParameterCombinedParameter, hmenum.ParameterLevelCombined }`. hmenum values match the backends literals exactly (pkg/hmenum/parameter.go:43 `ParameterCombinedParameter Parameter = "COMBINED_PARAMETER"`, :87 `ParameterLevelCombined Parameter = "LEVEL_COMBINED"`), so the three sets have identical membership TODAY. LIVENESS: backends is live (internal/central/adapter/callback_handlers.go:293 gates the whole combined-decompose path on backends.IsCombinedParameter). internal/parameter is live — the sole production caller is internal/client/interface_client_orchestration.go:324 `if paramconvert.IsConvertable(parameter) { ... AddCombinedParameter(...) }` inside WriteUnconfirmedValue. internal/model/value's copy has no production caller: grep for `IsConvertableParameter|ConvertableParameters` returns only tests/contract/convertable_parameter_parity_test.go, internal/model/value/converter_test.go, and the definitions. `grep -rn parameterLevelCombined --include=*.go .` shows the backends literals are referenced nowhere but combined.go — nothing imports hmenum to build them.

Both checks could have come back the other way; neither did.
stands.reason: Three declarations of one membership rule, two of them live on different paths of the same feature: parameter.IsConvertable decides whether a WRITE is decomposed into the command tracker (interface_client_orchestration.go:324), backends.IsCombinedParameter decides whether an incoming CALLBACK is decomposed into constituent data points (callback_handlers.go:293). Adding a third combined parameter to one and not the other leaves the write optimistically tracked as sub-parameters while the callback never decomposes it (or the reverse) — the value reaches the model in the wrong shape on exactly one of the two directions. The existing guard would stay green through that, because it pins the two sets that are NOT the ones that must agree at runtime (one of its two members, value's, has no production caller). Medium, not high: membership agrees today, and the failure needs a future edit to bite.
stands.divergence: None today — all three sets contain exactly {COMBINED_PARAMETER, LEVEL_COMBINED} and hmenum's string values equal the backends literals. The claim rests on the absence of any tie, not on a present disagreement.
stands.deadCopy: internal/model/value/converter.go:33 ConvertableParameters / :39 IsConvertableParameter — no production caller; referenced only from internal/model/value/converter_test.go:143 and tests/contract/convertable_parameter_parity_test.go. This is the copy the one existing guard is built around.
stands.guard: tests/contract/convertable_parameter_parity_test.go:22 TestConvertableParameterSetsAgree — pins internal/parameter against internal/model/value only. Nothing ties either to internal/client/backends/combined.go:26-27, and no test in tests/ references backends.IsCombinedParameter for set membership.
stands.secondReason: Survives. The three declarations exist verbatim at the cited lines, the enum strings and the raw literals are equal today, and no test ties the backends set to either of the others. The duplication is unforced: the backends package already imports pkg/hmenum elsewhere, so combined.go could use hmenum.ParameterCombinedParameter directly instead of its own string constants. The rest of the attack sharpens rather than kills it — the guard is not merely incomplete, it pins the live set (internal/parameter) to the one member that no daemon reads (internal/model/value), while the pairing that actually has to agree at runtime (internal/parameter on the write path, backends on the callback path) is unguarded. The claimed drift consequence is wrong in detail and right in kind: the failure is a silently dropped optimistic value, not a mis-shaped one. Medium is right — the sets agree today, so this needs a future edit to bite.

stands.title: The ReGa service/alarm/inbox message schemas are declared twice; the CcuBackend copies are unreachable from production and drop the URL-decoding contract

No production code calls InterfaceClient.GetServiceMessages, .GetAlarmMessages or .GetInboxDevices. The URL-encoding claim also holds: runner.go:314-315 documents `Name and Description are URL-encoded; callers should apply url.QueryUnescape before display` and the live reader honours it (hub_wiring.go:1489 `decodedName := decodeRegaField(m.Name)`, :1492 `DeviceName: decodeRegaField(m.DeviceName)`, :1499 `Rooms: decodeRegaFields(m.Rooms)`), while ccu_extended.go:250-251 emits `"name": m.Name` / `"device_name": m.DeviceName` raw with no decode anywhere in the function.
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false I would have found a production caller of InterfaceClient.GetServiceMessages / .GetAlarmMessages / .GetInboxDevices — a REST handler, MCP verb, or coordinator — in the greps over internal/north, internal/central, cmd and finally the whole repo; or the backends copies would have applied the same decodeRegaField the runner path applies, making the two readers behaviourally identical. stands.reason: One script output contract with two decoders, one of which is unreachable from any running daemon. A field added or renamed in get_service_messages.fn is picked up by whichever struct the author edits; the other decodes it as the zero value with no compile error and no test failure. The dead half makes it worse rather than better: internal/client/backends/ccu_extended_test.go:256/301 and ccu_jsonrpc_test.go:196 exercise the backends decoders and stay green, so the test suite reports coverage on a schema no production path reads, while the schema that IS read has its own separate tests. Medium: no operator-visible bug today (the live path is correct and applies the decode), but the drift surface is a wire contract with no guard and a documented semantic — URL encoding — that only one of the two copies carries.
stands.divergence: A ReGa `name` containing a non-ASCII character, e.g. a service message on a device named "Küche". The CCU emits it percent-encoded (get_service_messages.fn output is URL-encoded per runner.go:314-315), so the wire field is "K%FCche". The live path (hub_wiring.go:1489) returns `Name: "Küche"` via decodeRegaField; the backends path (ccu_extended.go:250) returns `"name": "K%FCche"` verbatim. Same script, same wire byte, two different values out.
stands.deadCopy: internal/client/backends/ccu_extended.go:227 (svcMsg), :310 (alarmMsg) and internal/client/backends/ccu.go:534 (inboxDevice) — reachable only through InterfaceClient.GetServiceMessages / .GetAlarmMessages / .GetInboxDevices (interface_client_orchestration.go:492/510) and CcuBackend's own methods, none of which has a non-test caller anywhere in the repo.
stands.guard: none. No test compares the backends structs to the rega ones; tests/contract/wiring_pins/ccu_wiring_test.go:14 only mentions "GetServiceMessages via ReGa" in a comment. tests/e2e/hub_aggregates_test.go:47 marks `"hub/service_messages": false` because godevccu does not serve it.
stands.secondReason: Survives. Every quote is exact and every line number current, the field sets are identical, and the liveness split is established by an exhaustive identifier grep rather than by inference: the runner copies are read on the boot/refresh path in hub_wiring.go, the backends copies are read by nothing outside _test.go. The best available defence is that internal/client/backends deliberately avoids importing internal/client/rega — caller.go:51-53 says so in as many words ("Declared here (consumer package) to keep backends free of a hard import of the rega package") — so a local decode shape is architecturally motivated. That defence does not save it, for two reasons. First, ccu_extended.go:813-819 shows the codebase reaching a runner-side domain method through a narrow interface assertion precisely to avoid re-implementing semantics behind that seam, so the boundary does not force the schema copy. stands.deadCopy: internal/client/interface_client.go:1082 — no production caller (internal/client/interface_client_test.go:186, internal/client/interface_client_deep_test.go:559 only). internal/routingkey/uniqueid.go:40 is live.

stands.title: The retry state machine exists twice (Do and DoForKey) with the schedule-advance rule copied three times
stands.evidence: Verified verbatim. retry.go:255 `func (r *Retrier) Do(ctx context.Context, fn func(ctx context.Context, attempt int) error) error {` and :498 `func (r *Retrier) DoForKey(ctx context.Context, key hmtypes.DataPointKey, fn func(ctx context.Context, attempt int) error) error { //nolint:funlen // single-purpose retry state machine with many error/backoff branches` — two full `for attempt := 1; attempt <= r.cfg.MaxAttempts; attempt++` loops. The schedule-advance conditional `if r.specialDelayFor(err) <= 0 { delay = nextDelay(delay, r.cfg.Multiplier, r.cfg.Max) }` appears at :327 (Do), :577 (DoForKey, recovery-wait branch) and :594 (DoForKey, timer branch) — grep for `specialDelayFor(err) <= 0` returns exactly those three lines. Both loops independently re-implement: the disabled fast-path, the ctx.Err() bail, isNonRetryableUnderConfig, the MaxAttempts exhaustion block with ExhaustedRetries + sink.ReportRetryExhausted + the identical `retry: exhausted after %d attempts: %w` wrapper, TotalRetries, specialDelayFor/jitter selection, and the RecoveryWaiter shortcut with recoveryDeadline. Both are live: Do from internal/client/interface_client.go:484 and :557; DoForKey from internal/client/interface_client_orchestration.go:745 (setValue) and :800 (putParamset). Guard: none — the retry tests (retry_lifecycle_test.go, retry_supersede_test.go, retry_cancel_count_test.go) exercise each entry point separately; no test asserts the two share a policy.
stands.negativeControl: Had the policy lived in one place, DoForKey would delegate to Do (or both to a shared loop) and the schedule-advance conditional would appear once. Reading the file, `grep -n 'specialDelayFor(err) <= 0' internal/client/reliability/retry.go` returns three lines in two functions, and lines 267-330 and 527-596 are two independent attempt loops.
stands.reason: Confirmed as duplication of the retry policy, unguarded, with both copies live and one of them (DoForKey) owning the setValue/putParamset write path. The candidate's remark that the two are already textually different is accurate — DoForKey `continue`s at :578 after the recovery wait while Do falls through at :318-320 — but I traced both and they are behaviourally equivalent: Do's fall-through reaches the same advance conditional at :327 and then the loop head, exactly what DoForKey's :577 + `continue` does. So no diverging input exists today; the only structural differences (supersede slot, cancel channel) are DoForKey's stated purpose. Severity medium on drift risk rather than a present defect: a backoff or exhaustion-accounting change applied to Do alone leaves every device write on the old policy, and nothing goes red.
stands.divergence: None found. I compared the two loops statement by statement and could not construct an input where they behave differently: the recovery-wait `continue` at :578 and Do's fall-through at :318-320 both land on the schedule-advance conditional and then the next attempt. The cancel-channel checks at :528-535 and :585-590 are DoForKey-only by design (ErrRetrySuperseded), not a policy disagreement.
stands.deadCopy: Neither. Do is called at internal/client/interface_client.go:484 and :557; DoForKey at internal/client/interface_client_orchestration.go:745 and :800.
stands.guard: none
stands.secondReason: Survives every bite. Quote and line numbers verified. Sameness: this is not one datum read two ways — it is one state machine transcribed, proven by a statement-level diff in which no policy line differs. Nothing in the type system forces the copy: a shared body taking a `cancel <-chan struct{}` (nil for Do, where a nil channel simply never selects) would unify them. Liveness: both copies are on production paths, and the copy that is *not* the primary one owns every device write. Divergence: none today — I could not construct one either, so this is drift risk, not a present defect, and medium is the right severity. Damage: visible and unguarded. A change to backoff, jitter, exhaustion accounting or the recovery-wait deadline applied to Do alone leaves setValue/putParamset on the old schedule, and nothing goes red — the DoForKey tests never touch that policy, so the drift is invisible to the suite as well as to the reader. The triple copy of the advance rule (:327, :577, :594) is the same hazard one level down: a fix to the special-delay carve-out has to be made in three places inside one file.

stands.title: Non-finite doubles are rejected on the BIN-RPC write, BIN-RPC read and XML-RPC read paths, but not on the XML-RPC write path
stands.divergence: One value, one shared producer, two answers: goToXMLRPCValue (internal/central/adapter/xmlrpc_caller.go:80, and the same function reached from binrpc_caller.go:33) turns a float64 NaN into xmlrpc.DoubleValue(NaN). Over BIN-RPC that value hits encode.go:113 "case xmlrpc.DoubleValue: return writeDouble(...)" → encodeDouble → error "binrpc: NaN is not representable", and the write never leaves the daemon. Over XML-RPC the identical value marshals to the literal body <double>NaN.0</double> and is sent to the device (+Inf → <double>+Inf.0</double>, -Inf → <double>-Inf.0</double>; a finite 1 → <double>1.0</double>).
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false I would have found either (a) a math.IsNaN/IsInf rejection inside DoubleValue.MarshalXML or in writeTagged/the MethodCall marshaller upstream of it — grep for IsNaN/IsInf across internal/client returns hits only at binrpc/encode.go:243,246, binrpc/decode.go:175, xmlrpc/decode.go:139, rega/runner.go:389,391 — or (b) FormatFloat emitting a string containing '.' for NaN, which the toolchain source at internal/strconv/ftoa.go:97 rules out. Both checks would have produced a different, visible result.
stands.guard: none on the XML-RPC write side; the three sibling sites each have one (TestEncodeRejectsNaN, TestEncodedoubleRejectsNaN, TestDecodeValueNonFiniteDoubleRejected)
stands.reason: The invariant is real and enforced three times; the fourth site is missing it, and the two write sides give demonstrably different answers to the same xmlrpc.DoubleValue. Severity medium rather than high because the malformed literal is rejected by the CCU's own validator rather than silently mis-applied (value.go:142-144 documents fault -5 for a double the validator dislikes), and reaching it needs a bad payload (MQTT "nan", or a NaN produced upstream) rather than normal traffic. The xmlrpc decode comment naming binrpc encodeDouble as its model makes the gap read as covered, which is why it survived.
stands.secondReason: Survives. The quote is current, both write sites are live (xmlrpcCaller and binrpcCaller share goToXMLRPCValue verbatim — binrpc_caller.go:33 calls the same function), and the diverging input is reachable end to end without a crafted internal state: an MQTT command payload of "nan" on a FLOAT parameter parses to float64 NaN, survives coercion (NaN fails every range comparison), and reaches the marshaller. Over BIN-RPC that same xmlrpc.DoubleValue is refused locally by writeDouble→encodeDouble (encode.go:166-173, :243-248); over XML-RPC it is serialised as the literal <double>NaN.0</double> and put on the wire. One caveat I record rather than hide, because it weakens the framing without killing the finding: the three sibling guards do not all enforce one rule. binrpc encodeDouble's own comment justifies itself by representability ("the format cannot represent them precisely"), and both decode guards justify themselves by north-bound JSON encodability of a value entering the model — neither rationale applies to a value leaving the daemon as XML text. So the strongest form of this finding is not "a fourth copy of one guard is missing" but "the XML-RPC write path emits a literal that is not a valid XML-RPC double", which stands on its own. Severity medium as filed: the malformed literal is rejected downstream rather than silently applied, and it needs a bad payload rather than normal traffic.

stands.deadCopy: internal/config/schedule_timer.go (ScheduleTimerConfig, DefaultScheduleTimerConfig, WithDefaults) and internal/config/timeouts.go (TimeoutConfig, DefaultTimeoutConfig, WithDefaults) — no production caller anywhere; the live path is internal/central/jobs.go:177-203.
stands.guard: internal/config/schedule_timer_test.go and internal/config/timeouts_test.go pin the dead copy. No guard asserts either type is reachable from Config or that its values match jobs.go.
stands.secondReason: Survives as a dead-copy finding, which the brief rates stronger, not weaker: TestDefaultScheduleTimerConfigNonZero / TestDefaultTimeoutConfigNonZero and their WithDefaults twins keep both copies permanently green while the daemon runs on jobs.go. Two corrections to the candidate's damage text, neither fatal. (1) The divergence sentence misdescribes the mechanism: there is no `schedule_timer` key in the config schema at all — the type is not a field of Config — so an operator does not set an ignored key, the key does not exist, and yaml.Unmarshal drops the whole block without a word. Nothing documents it either, so the realistic reader is a developer reading the Go source, not an operator copying YAML. (2) The TimeoutConfig half is weaker than the ScheduleTimerConfig half: there is no single live TimeoutConfig-shaped policy to be a copy OF. The live values are per-transport and differently shaped — internal/client/transport/xmlrpc/client.go:24 "const DefaultTimeout = 30 * time.Second", internal/client/transport/jsonrpc/client.go:32 same, internal/client/transport/binrpc/client.go:23 "DefaultDialTimeout = 5 * time.Second" and :27 "DefaultIOTimeout = 15 * time.Second", internal/client/state_change.go:63 "timeout = 60 * time.Second". TimeoutConfig.Connect = 10s has no source-carried peer at all, so I decline to call it a divergent duplicate of any specific constant — it is dead, not provably duplicated.
