stands.title: The bootstrap tier and the full tier each carry their own copy of the same defaults and the same logging acceptance sets
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false, one tier would reference the other — a shared `const defaultDataDir` / `validLogLevels` set, or BootstrapConfig.applyDefaults delegating to a common helper — and grep for the literals would return a single definition site. Instead `grep -rn '"./var"|":8119"'` over internal/ and cmd/ (excluding tests) returns three independent assignment sites (bootstrap.go:139/148, config.go:1894/1915, cmd/hmcli/cache.go:408) and the level/format branches are duplicated in full. No test compares the two tiers: grep for "Bootstrap" across internal/config/config_test.go and tests/contract/ returns only an unrelated router-deps string.
stands.reason: One policy (the accepted logging enumerations and the four boot defaults) written out three times with no shared constant, in a package where both writers are live and read at different moments of the same boot. Because the two error strings are identical — both "config: invalid logging.level %q" — a rejection names the field but not the tier, exactly as the candidate says. No guard exists. Severity medium: nothing diverges today, so no operator is currently affected; the cost is realised on the next edit to either list, and the failure mode (hmcli and the daemon resolving different data directories) is the one the DefaultWithEnv / OverlayFromEnv comments at bootstrap.go:155-163 already document as having happened once for the env overlay.
stands.divergence: None today — the four defaults and both acceptance sets are byte-identical across the two tiers, and the hmcli fallback is currently unreachable because config.LoadWithEnv has already run applyDefaults (so cfg.DataDir is never "" at cmd/hmcli/cache.go:407). Latent: adding a "trace" level to config.go:2038 alone makes `logging.level: trace` load the daemon and abort hmcli's LoadBootstrap with "config: invalid logging.level \"trace\""; changing the default data dir in config.go:1894 alone leaves hmcli's LoadBootstrap path and cmd/hmcli/cache.go:408 pointing at "./var".
stands.deadCopy: Neither of the two cited tiers — ParseBootstrap (cmd/openccu-loom/main.go:87, backup.go:991) and Config.Parse (config.go:1838) are both live. The third copy at cmd/hmcli/cache.go:408 is effectively dead code (its guard cannot be true after LoadWithEnv), which makes it the one most likely to drift unnoticed.
stands.guard: None. No test in internal/config or tests/contract compares BootstrapConfig.applyDefaults/Validate against Config.applyDefaults/Validate.
stands.secondReason: Confirmed, and the sameness bite fails hardest here: both tiers validate the domain of ONE shared type (config.LoggingConfig, bootstrap.go:39), so this is not two rules sharing a shape and the type system does not force the repetition — a method on LoggingConfig would carry it. Three corrections to the candidate, one of which replaces its damage story with a worse one. (a) The hmcli claim is false: hmcli never calls LoadBootstrap — the only production callers are cmd/openccu-loom/backup.go:991 and cmd/openccu-loom/main.go:87. cmd/hmcli/cache.go:407-408 "dataDir := cfg.DataDir; if dataDir == \"\" { dataDir = \"./var\" }" is an independent literal, unrelated to the bootstrap tier. (b) "three times" is wrong in both directions: the acceptance sets appear twice, while "./var" appears in eleven production files (cmd/hmcli/cache.go:408, cmd/openccu-loom/{public_url.go:31, descriptor_stores_wiring.go:30, audit_wiring.go:57, master_values_wiring.go:27, values_cache_wiring.go:31, daemon_boot.go:110, visibility_wiring.go:30, history_wiring.go:32,66}, plus internal/config/{config.go:1894, bootstrap.go:139}) — DefaultBootstrap (bootstrap.go:102-106) is not a third copy, it just calls applyDefaults. (c) The real damage on a one-sided level edit is subtler and worse than claimed: adding "trace" to config.go:2038 alone makes `openccu-loom backup ...` abort with "config: invalid logging.level \"trace\"" (backup.go:1001) while the daemon boots fine, AND main.go:87 discards the bootstrap parse error entirely (`perr == nil` guard), so the operator's `env_file:` setting is silently ignored and every env-sourced secret goes missing with no log line at all.

stands.title: Two contradictory answers for 'how many week programs does this thermostat have'
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false, ScheduleProfileNos would have delegated to numWeekPrograms (or to the descriptor) rather than to profileWeekIndex over six literals, and the repo-wide grep would have named at least one caller outside a _test.go file. Neither is the case.
stands.reason: The two functions answer the same question by contradictory methods, and the exported one is the wrong one. Concrete diverging inputs exist at the code level (see divergence), needing no device convention: SupportsProfile is a static capability set (init.go:130-134 rfCapabilities, :115 ipCapabilities — both true) that is independent of whether the pointer DP or its descriptor exists. Severity medium and not low despite the dead caller: it is an exported method on a public model type, it reads as authoritative, and its only test (climate_commands_test.go:713) asserts merely >0 versus ==0, so it would stay green at any nonzero count — a future caller would adopt the wrong answer without any gate reacting.
stands.guard: none — TestScheduleProfileNos (internal/model/custom/climate/climate_commands_test.go:713-733) checks only `n > 0` vs `n == 0`, so it never observes the count.
stands.divergence: A KindRF Climate built with rfCapabilities (SupportsProfile=true, init.go:134) whose channel resolves a WEEK_PROGRAM_POINTER DP with descriptor MIN=0 / MAX=2: numWeekPrograms() = min(max(int(2-0)+1,0),6) = 3, so payload.go:256-269 publishes three week-program presets, while ScheduleProfileNos() returns 6. Same shape with no pointer DP at all and a non-nil channelRef (climate.go:2341-2356 → return 0): numWeekPrograms() = 0, zero week-program presets published, ScheduleProfileNos() = 6.
stands.deadCopy: ScheduleProfileNos — internal/model/custom/climate/climate.go:2060; sole caller is internal/model/custom/climate/climate_commands_test.go:726.
stands.secondReason: Every load-bearing fact checked out and the attack failed on each bite. Quote: current and verbatim. Sameness: these are not one datum read two ways for two callers — ScheduleProfileNos's own inline comment claims it counts "the week-program slots that would appear in Profiles()", and Profiles() (climate.go:607) derives that count from numWeekPrograms(), so the two are asserted by the code to answer one question and do not. Divergence: reproduced by reading both paths. With a non-nil channelRef resolving a WEEK_PROGRAM_POINTER whose descriptor is MIN=0/MAX=2, numWeekPrograms() = min(max(int(2-0)+1,0),6) = 3 while ScheduleProfileNos() = 6; with a non-nil channelRef and no pointer DP (the HM-CC-RT-DN shape named in the comment at climate.go:2331-2333) numWeekPrograms() = 0 while ScheduleProfileNos() = 6. Nothing upstream filters this: the descriptor MIN/MAX is read straight off the wire paramset and SupportsProfile is a literal. Damage is where the finding overstates itself, so I downgraded medium to low: ScheduleProfileNos has zero production callers, the package is internal/ (not a public Go API surface as the claim implies), and no wire, MQTT or REST output changes today. What survives is real but latent: an exported method returning a knowingly wrong count, a doc comment describing behaviour it does not have, and a guard (climate_commands_test.go:713-733, asserting only >0 vs ==0) that cannot react to any nonzero answer. A fourth, unclaimed defect is adjacent and worth folding in: notes/parity/by_design.md:3410-3416 blesses the static behaviour under the heading "Climate.ScheduleProfileNos uses static 1..6 pool" but its body and its "Go path" line both name numWeekPrograms — the descriptor-driven function — so the divergence register documents the wrong function and cites stale line numbers (climate.go:1808-1840).

stands.title: Matter temperature and humidity encoders are byte-for-byte duplicated between the climate projection and the measurement cluster
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false, the two bodies would differ in rounding, clamp bound or comment, or one would call the other / a shared exported helper. Both are unexported in different packages, so no shared source exists, and a diff of the two nine-line bodies is empty. Had humidityToMatter been live, the grep would have named a non-test caller and MatterClusterServers would list a humidity server.
stands.reason: The temperature half is duplication between two live paths that encode the same physical reading for the same device: the climate comment at matter.go:255-260 itself records that the channel's ACTUAL_TEMPERATURE materialises as its own TemperatureSensor (0x0302) endpoint through the generic measurement path, so one reading is encoded by both copies onto two endpoints of the same bridge. A second rounding/clamp fix therefore has two landing sites, and the only thing binding them is a prose comment. The humidity half is worse in kind: internal/model/custom/climate/matter.go:209 has no production caller, so its two tests stay green while every real humidity value goes through measurement.humidityToUint16 — a copy that a maintainer would reasonably edit believing it reaches the wire.
stands.guard: none — no cross-package test compares the two encoders; each side is pinned separately (internal/model/custom/climate/climate_internals_test.go:1389-1420 for celsiusToMatter; internal/north/matter/cluster/measurement/measurement_test.go:98-123 for the TemperatureServer clamps).
stands.divergence: none found — the four functions agree on every input today; the two temperature bodies are token-identical, as are the two humidity bodies.
stands.deadCopy: humidityToMatter — internal/model/custom/climate/matter.go:209; callers only internal/model/custom/climate/climate_internals_test.go:1426/:1429 and internal/model/custom/climate/matter_test.go:559. celsiusToMatter is live.
stands.secondReason: The finding survived every bite. Quote: verified verbatim, line numbers current. Sameness: this is not the EnumLabel/EnumLabelFromWire shape where one datum is read two ways for two callers — both encode a float °C (or %RH) into Matter's int16/uint16 centi-unit representation with the same 0x8000-null-avoidance clamp, and the climate copy's own doc comment at matter.go:187-189 says so: "Matches internal/north/matter/cluster/measurement celsiusToInt16, the encoder behind the standalone TemperatureMeasurement endpoints." That comment is the only binding between the two, which is exactly the defect. Type system does not force it: both are plain float64→integer helpers, and climate already imports three packages from the same north/matter subtree. Liveness and damage split by half. Temperature half: both copies live, so a second rounding or clamp correction has two landing sites and drift is observable — the thermostat endpoint's LocalTemperature and the sensor endpoint's MeasuredValue would report different hundredths for the same reading. Humidity half is the stronger one and the reason I keep this at medium: humidityToMatter has no production caller while every real humidity value goes through measurement.humidityToUint16, so a maintainer fixing rounding or clamping in the climate copy would change nothing on the wire and would be told it worked by two green tests (climate_internals_test.go:1426-1431, matter_test.go:559). One qualifier the claim overstates and I could not fully verify: that one ACTUAL_TEMPERATURE reading is definitely encoded twice onto two endpoints of the same bridged device. The mapping half is verified in code (internal/model/generic/matter.go:43-44 routes ParameterActualTemperature/ParameterTemperature to MatterMeasurementTemperature, and measurement.go:889-891 turns that into a TemperatureServer), but whether a thermostat channel's own ACTUAL_TEMPERATURE data point survives the endpoint-candidate visibility gate on that device I did not trace end to end — the claim's support for that step is the prose comment at matter.go:255-260, which is a hypothesis, not evidence. The duplication finding does not rest on it.

stands.title: The RF-lock STATE polarity is restated at three sites (read, write, HA discovery)
stands.evidence: All three quotes verified verbatim. Read path, lock.go:349-352: `if v {` / `\treturn StateUnlocked, true` / `}` / `return StateLocked, true`. Write path, lock.go:558-566: `// KindRF uses the bool STATE parameter: false locks, true unlocks.` / `case commandLock:` / `\tif err := l.writer.SetValue(ctx, l.Address, hmenum.ParameterState, false, priority); …` / `case commandUnlock:` / `\t… hmenum.ParameterState, true, priority)`. HA payload, payload.go:177-180: `// RF locks expose a bool STATE: false = locked, true = unlocked.` / `commandTopic = ctx.WireParameterCommandTopic("STATE")` / `payloadLock = "false"` / `payloadUnlock = "true"`. The three are genuinely independent: the HA payload names a *wire-parameter* command topic, so a Home-Assistant lock command writes STATE directly and never passes through sendRF — the two write paths only agree because both spell the polarity out. All three are live (sendRF is the KindRF branch of Lock's command dispatch; LockState is the state accessor; HADiscoveryPayload is the MQTT discovery body).
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false I would have found the RF polarity expressed once and referenced — the way the *IP* case already is: payload.go:200-201 uses `payloadLock = ipTargetLocked` / `payloadUnlock = ipTargetUnlocked`, the same constants sendIP writes. For RF, payload.go carries the string literals "false"/"true" and lock.go carries the bool literals false/true, with no shared symbol.
stands.reason: Three live restatements of one firmware fact, with no cross-check. The strongest evidence is that the repo already solved this exact problem one Kind over: tests/contract/lock_target_level_payload_parity_test.go:78 TestLockTargetLevelDiscoveryPayloadsMatchServiceWrites crosses advertised payload against wire write and asserts no literal of its own — and its header says the untied spelling is what let the IP pair drift before. That guard is constructed with `Kind: lock.KindIP` (line 85) only; there is no RF equivalent, and nothing ties the read path to either writer for any Kind.
stands.guard: None crossing the three sites. Each is pinned separately against its own literal: lock_test.go:377 TestLockRFLockSendsStateFalse (write), payload_discovery_test.go:103 TestLockHADiscoveryPayload_KindRFUsesState (asserts payload_lock == "false"), lock_payload_test.go:85 TestState_BoolStateDPFalseIsLocked (read). A coherent set of three edits — production plus its own pin — passes all of them.
stands.divergence: None today; all three agree on false=locked.
stands.deadCopy: Neither — all three have production callers.
stands.secondReason: Survived every bite. The quotes are current and exact; all three sites are reachable from a registered production constructor and the live MQTT discovery path; the three are one firmware fact (bool STATE: true = unlocked) spelled three times rather than one datum read two ways — the read and the two writers agree today only by coincidence of maintenance. Drift is observable and safety-relevant: flip the payload literals alone and Home Assistant's lock button unlocks a door while daemon-issued commands still lock it; flip the read alone and the same door reports locked while open. The repo already treats this exact shape as worth tying one Kind over (the IP parity guard's header names the untied spelling as what let IP drift), and the RF equivalent is absent. The type mismatch (bool wire value vs. string MQTT payload vs. State enum) is real but does not force the repetition — a shared bool constant rendered with strconv.FormatBool covers all three.

stands.title: The group-slot binding walk is written three times, and each stops at the first entry of a Go map
stands.evidence: Quotes exact. cover/init.go:182-184 `for chNo, fields := range rebased.ChannelFields {` / `\tfv, ok := fields[hmenum.FieldGroupLevel]` / `\tif !ok {`; cover/init.go:205-207 `if dp := custom.GroupLevelField(groupCh, param); dp != nil {` / `\tcov.SetGroupLevel(dp, useGroupChannelForState(ch))` / `\treturn`; valve/init.go:53-54 `for chNo, fields := range rebased.ChannelFields {` / `\tfv, ok := fields[hmenum.FieldGroupState]`; profile_schema.go:153 `ChannelFields map[int]map[hmenum.Field]FieldValue`. All copies are live: cover's are called from the registered constructors (init.go:151, :152, :165, :275, :276, :290), valve's from valve/init.go:33, switch's from switch/init.go:85 and :94, light's from light/init.go:235, :266, :297, :312. Each copy also re-inlines the sibling-channel lookup (`for _, sibling := range ch.Device().Channels() { if sibling.Number == chNo {`) that light/init.go:217 already factored out as `siblingChannel`.
stands.negativeControl: Had the walk been written once I would have found the three call sites delegating to one helper in internal/model/custom (alongside ResolveSlotOr / GroupLevelField, which they do share for the leaf steps). Instead each of the five functions repeats the loop, the field lookup, the ResolveFieldValue guard and the sibling scan in full.
stands.reason: Confirmed, and stronger than filed: the count is five, not three, and two of the copies ALREADY disagree. light/init.go:190 checks the group-wide block first — `if fv, ok := rebased.Fields[hmenum.FieldGroupLevel]; ok {` … `l.SetGroupLevel(dp)` — before falling through to the ChannelFields walk; the cover, valve and switch copies never read rebased.Fields at all, so a profile declaring the field group-wide binds nothing on those paths. The comment at light/init.go:185-189 records that reading only one of the two blocks 'missed every HmIP device'. Separately, none of the five consults FixedChannelFields (profile_schema.go:156). The map-iteration point is verified as latent, read from the source rather than assumed: profile_configs.go carries these fields at :75-76 (ChannelFields{-1:{GroupLevel, GroupLevel2}}), :124, :152 (ChannelFields{-1:{GroupLevel}}), :219, :434 (ChannelFields{-1:{GroupState}}) and :611/:631/:651/:678/:698 (in the group-wide Fields block, ChannelFields nil) — that enumeration is complete for the three fields, and no profile maps one of them at two offsets, so the first-hit return is deterministic today.
stands.guard: None. No test constructs a profile whose group field appears at two channel offsets, and none compares the five copies' behaviour on one input.
stands.divergence: A profile that declares the group field in the group-wide `Fields` block instead of `ChannelFields`. That shape ships today for lights: profile_configs.go:611 `hmenum.FieldGroupLevel: Visible(hmenum.ParameterLevelReal)` inside `Fields:` with `ChannelFields: nil` (RfDimmer; likewise :631, :651, :678, :698). Fed to light/init.go:190 it binds LEVEL_REAL on the primary channel; fed to the byte-identical shape in cover/init.go:182 or valve/init.go:53 it binds nothing and the group DP stays nil. No cover/valve/switch profile carries that shape at present, so the divergence is reachable but not currently exercised.
stands.deadCopy: None — all five have production callers.
stands.secondReason: The duplication survives; two of the finding's three damage claims do not, so the severity drops to low. Confirmed: five live copies, valve's and switch's identical apart from the receiver name, all five re-implementing a subset of an existing, better repo helper (ResolveFieldSlot), with the classic drift signature already present — a fix applied to one copy only, light/init.go:190, whose own comment says the missing branch 'missed every HmIP device' on the other paths. Refuted within the finding: the map-iteration nondeterminism is latent, not live (every group-field ChannelFields block has one key, and rebasing is 1:1), and the claimed divergent input cannot occur with shipping data — no cover, valve or switch profile declares the group field group-wide, so all five copies are behaviour-equivalent today. I also checked the sentinel rather than assuming it: `AnyChannelOffset = math.MinInt32` (profile_schema.go:22, with :16 `// We deliberately do not reuse -1 (which is [hmenum.ChannelOffsetState])`), so the `-1:` keys are genuine rebased offsets and the copies do bind — there is no hidden live failure behind them either.

stands.title: The LEVEL-to-0..255 brightness rule exists twice and the two forms disagree (truncate vs round)
stands.evidence: Both quotes verbatim. payload.go:97-99 `if b, ok := l.Brightness(); ok {` / `\t\tv := int(b.Level()*255 + 0.5)` / `\t\tstate.Brightness = &v`. mixins.go:465-466 `// Byte returns the value as 0–255.` / `func (b Brightness) Byte() uint8 { return uint8(b.level * 255) }`. Both live: payload.go:98 is the MQTT state payload, published via internal/north/mqtt/bridge.go:1059 `state := src.State()` inside PublishSourceState; Byte() is called from light.go:566 `b := custom.NewBrightness(level).Byte()` in SetLevel and light.go:955 `if b, ok := l.commandedBrightness(); !ok || b.Byte() != *brightness {` in IsStateChange. The HA command path divides by 255 at payload.go:313 and :327 (`l.SetLevel(ctx, f/255.0, priority)`). The doc-comment the candidate cites is real, at light.go:816-819 (not 837-843): "The conversion itself belongs to the value object — see [custom.Brightness.Pct] — so a light and a group report the same percentage for the same level. A device profile composes value objects; it is not a second place for the arithmetic."
stands.negativeControl: Had State() used the shared rule, payload.go:98 would read `b.Byte()` and the level sweep would report 0 disagreeing levels. It reports 500 of 1001 — and had the disagreement been cosmetic (never re-arming a write), the echo leg of the same sweep would have reported 0 re-arms; it reports 500 of 500.
stands.reason: Two live forms of one rule that already disagree on half the CCU's LEVEL grid, with a measurable consequence on the write path: every HA brightness echo at a disagreeing level defeats the redundant-command suppression and issues a real CCU write. The base Light's own doc-comment (light.go:816-819) states the arithmetic must not be duplicated, and it is.
stands.divergence: level = 0.5: State() publishes brightness 128 (int(0.5*255+0.5) = int(128.0)); Brightness.Byte() returns 127 (uint8(127.5), Go truncates toward zero). Swept the CCU's 0.001 LEVEL grid: the two forms disagree on 500 of 1001 levels, and for all 500 the round trip re-arms a write — echo the published byte b, SetLevel(b/255) computes Byte(b/255) = b, which differs from the commanded byte derived from the raw level, so IsStateChange (light.go:955) returns true and SetLevel writes to the CCU again. Worked case: level 0.5 → publish 128 → HA echoes 128 → SetLevel(128/255 = 0.5019607843137255) → Byte = uint8(128.0) = 128 ≠ commanded 127 → redundant write. First disagreeing levels: 0.002 (State 1, Byte 0), 0.003 (1 vs 0), 0.006 (2 vs 1), 0.007 (2 vs 1).
stands.guard: brightness_pct_agreement_test.go pins only the percentage path, and its own doc says so: "It compares the accessors against each other, so a change to the shared rule moves all three together and stays green — it enforces a single source, not a particular rounding. And none of the three has a production caller today." internal/model/custom/extra_test.go:199 pins `b.Byte() != 127` for level 0.5; internal/model/custom/custom_test.go:75 deliberately accepts either 127 or 128. Nothing compares the State() byte against Byte().
stands.deadCopy: Neither side is dead. (Adjacent observation, not the finding: Light.GroupBrightness (light.go:369), the third Byte() caller, has no production caller outside light.go — every hit is in _test.go.)
stands.secondReason: One rule (level → HA 0–255 brightness) in two forms that disagree on half the grid, with a traced consequence on the write path. Worked case, both paths read end to end: device level 0.5 → State() publishes brightness `int(0.5*255+0.5)` = 128 (payload.go:98) → HA echoes 128 → applyHASetLevel calls SetLevel(128/255 = 0.5019607843137255) (payload.go:313) → SetLevel computes `b = Byte(0.50196…)` = uint8(128.0) = 128 (light.go:566) → IsStateChange compares against `commandedBrightness().Byte()` = uint8(0.5*255) = uint8(127.5) = 127 (light.go:955) → 127 != 128 → returns true → the redundant-command suppression is defeated and SetLevel writes LEVEL to the CCU. Neither form is forced by the type system (Byte returns uint8, the payload wants int, but `int(b.Byte())` would compile), and the divergence is observable on two surfaces: the published MQTT brightness for a given level differs by one from the byte every comparison and every other accessor uses (light.go:369 GroupBrightness also goes through Byte()).

stands.title: The OnOff cluster constant block and the LT GlobalSceneControl state machine are implemented twice, in light and in switch
stands.evidence: Quotes verbatim, two cited light line numbers off by 2-3 (matterAttrClusterRevision is at :108 not :111; matterOnOffClusterRevision at :129 not :130; the coercions at :907-940 not :914-921). light/matter.go:49 `matterClusterOnOff        uint32 = 0x0006`, :108 `matterAttrClusterRevision uint32 = 0xFFFD`, :129 `matterOnOffClusterRevision uint16 = 6`; switch/matter.go:37 `matterClusterOnOff uint32 = 0x0006`, :41 `matterAttrClusterRevision uint32 = 0xFFFD`, :71 `matterOnOffClusterRevision uint16 = 6`. Both files declare their own identical errMatterUnknownAttribute / errMatterUnknownCommand / errMatterValueType (light:144-146, switch:75-77), the same six command IDs 0x00/0x01/0x02/0x40/0x41/0x42 (light:112-121, switch:60-69), the same four LT attribute IDs 0x4000-0x4003 (light:71-74, switch:51-54), the same FeatureMap bit `matterFeatureOnOffLT uint32 = 0x01` (light:85, switch:59), and their own matterWriteUint16/matterWriteUint8 (light:933/938 delegating to wireUint16/wireUint8 at :907-927; switch:377/390 hand-rolled). No cross-import. Both are live: lightOnOffServer.MatterClusterID (light/matter.go:215) and Switch.MatterClusterID (switch/matter.go:110) are both reached through interfaces.MatterEndpointSource by the bridge assembler.
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false, one file would import the other's constants, or both would import the shared internal/north/matter/cluster/wire block or the generated schema table. grep shows two independent `const (…0x0006…)` blocks and two independent errMatter* var blocks, and neither package imports the other.
stands.reason: Two live copies of one cluster's identity and LT semantics, in the subtree whose stated rule is that Matter constants come from one place because drift causes silent pair-aborts — and the copies have already diverged behaviourally. Severity is medium rather than high because the two revision constants are each anchored to the same matter.js snapshot by their own parity test, so a numeric revision drift is caught; the LT behaviour and the switch's attribute set are not covered by anything.
stands.divergence: Behaviour, not values. OnWithTimedOff (0x42) with OnTime = 100 (10.0 s): a bridged light turns on and autonomously off after 10 s while OnTime counts 100 → 0, driven by the real engine in light/matter_timed_onoff.go:19-38 (`matterTimedTickInterval = 100 * time.Millisecond`, transliterating OnOffServer.ts). A bridged plug turns on and stays on forever — switch/matter.go:298-303 `// OnWithTimedOff (LT, mandatory): no on-timer, so the timed-off` / `// semantics are dropped and the switch is turned on.` — and its OnTime attribute, written at :211-221 and read at :141-145 (`return uint16(s.onTime.Load() & 0xFFFF), true`), never decrements: there is no time.Ticker anywhere under internal/model/custom/switch/. The Switch type does carry TurnOnFor / SetTimerOnTime (switch/switch.go:223, :236), so this is a gap rather than a capability limit, and notes/parity/by_design.md carries no entry for it. Second, already-drifted divergence in the same copy family: the coercion helper exists a third time in internal/model/custom/cover/matter.go:875-885, where wireUint16 accepts `case uint8: return uint16(n), true` — the light's wireUint16 (light/matter.go:919-927) rejects uint8. Input uint8(5): cover returns (5, true), light returns (0, false).
stands.guard: TestParityMatterJS_LightClusterRevisions (light/parity_matterjs_test.go:223) and TestParityMatterJS_SwitchClusterRevisions (switch/parity_matterjs_test.go:69) each anchor their own matterOnOffClusterRevision against the same matter.js schema snapshot, so a one-sided revision edit IS caught — the candidate's revision-drift damage is over-stated. Nothing pins the switch's OnOff attribute set against matter.js (its only other parity test is NoSpuriousOptions, :55), and nothing pins the LT behaviour of the two implementations against each other.
stands.deadCopy: internal/north/matter/cluster/wire/onoff.go:15-20 declares the same six OnOff command IDs (OnOffCmdOff/On/Toggle/OffWithEffect/OnWithRecallGlobalScene/OnWithTimedOff) and has NO caller at all — production or test: grep for each identifier returns only the declaration lines. A third copy that nothing exercises. Separately, internal/north/matter/schema/clusters.go:16 `0x0006: 6,  // OnOff` is the *generated* matter.js revision ("Code generated by script/generate_matter_schema.go … DO NOT EDIT"), but in production it is consumed only by the REST diagnostics view (cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_matter.go:4077 `if rev, ok := matterschema.ClusterRevision(id); ok`), never by the wire path — so the generated table and the wire answer are two unlinked sources for the same number.
stands.secondReason: Same cluster identity and same LT semantics, implemented twice in a subtree whose stated rule is that Matter constants come from one place, and the copies have already diverged behaviourally where nothing measures them. OnWithTimedOff (0x42) with OnTime = 100: a bridged light runs the transliterated matter.js countdown (matter_timed_onoff.go:19-38, ticking every 100 ms), a bridged plug turns on and stays on — switch/matter.go:297-299 `// OnWithTimedOff (LT, mandatory): no on-timer, so the timed-off` / `// semantics are dropped and the switch is turned on.` — and its OnTime attribute is stored (`s.onTime.Store(uint32(v))`, :219) and read back unchanged (`return uint16(s.onTime.Load() & 0xFFFF), true`, :145) with nothing to decrement it. Both endpoints advertise the same LT bit, so a controller sees the same contract and gets two behaviours; Switch already has the device-side capability (TurnOnFor, switch/switch.go:223, which bundles ON_TIME + STATE into one put_paramset, and SetTimerOnTime at :236), so this is an unwired gap, not a capability limit. The parity tests pin only the revision numbers against the matter.js snapshot (switch/parity_matterjs_test.go, light/parity_matterjs_test.go), so numeric drift is caught while the behavioural drift is not. One sub-claim does not survive: the wireUint16 difference (cover/matter.go:875-885 accepts `case uint8`, light/matter.go:919-927 does not) cannot diverge in production — both files document that the IM write layer delivers decoded TLV unsigned ints as uint64 (light/matter.go:903-906, cover/matter.go:871-874: `The uint16/uint8 cases keep the helper usable from tests that pass narrower Go types directly`), and the only production callers pass values from that layer (light/matter.go:290, :959, :966; cover/matter.go:842). Treat that one as a test affordance, not drift.

stands.title: The CCU timer (value, unit) encoding is implemented twice, and the two implementations disagree on truncation
stands.evidence:
Quotes verified verbatim. timer.go:27 `const timerUpperBoundSeconds = 16343`; mixins.go:136 `const timeUnitThreshold = 16343` — the same number declared twice. timer.go:373-388 `func RecalcUnit(seconds float64) (float64, hmenum.TimerUnit) { ... if seconds <= timerUpperBoundSeconds { return seconds, hmenum.TimerUnitSeconds } minutes := seconds / 60 ... return seconds / 3600, hmenum.TimerUnitHours }` returns float64 and keeps the fraction. mixins.go:219-250 `func EncodeTimerDuration(d time.Duration) (value, unit int32)` ends `return clamp(t), u` with `clamp` doing `return int32(v)` — truncation toward zero, documented at mixins.go:216-218.

Both sides are live and write the SAME two parameters on the SAME channel. combined.NewTimer has exactly one production call site: siren.go:142-146 `s.duration = combined.NewTimer(address, cfg.Writer, hmenum.ParameterDurationValue, hmenum.ParameterDurationUnit)`. Its SetDuration (timer.go:248-256) writes UnitParameter then ValueParameter, and is reached from production via projection.go:118 `return t.SetDuration(ctx, time.Duration(seconds*float64(time.Second)), priority)` in `WriteCombined`, whose only production caller is mqtt_sink.go:470 `return writable.WriteCombined(ctx, raw, priority)`. The other encoder is called at siren.go:328 `value, unit := custom.EncodeTimerDuration(cfg.Duration)` and siren.go:334/415, sound.go:377/382, light.go:873/883/1059, color.go:807.

The float64 reaches the wire uncoerced: Timer.Writer is the channel writer (siren/init.go:88 `Writer: channel.Writer()`), which chains device.Channel.Writer() -> channelWriterAdapter.SetValue (bound_writer.go:95) -> boundWriter.SetValue (bound_writer.go:71) -> client.ValueWriter.SetValue (value_writer.go:157), which calls SetValueWithOptions with `CheckAgainstPD false` (value_writer.go:164-165). In write_options.go:114-165 the value is only coerced inside `if opts.CheckAgainstPD`, then passed through unchanged to `b.SetValue(ctx, channelAddress, parameter, value, ...)`. parameter.Coerce is never on this path (its only production callers are devices.go:877 and paramsets.go:329/720).
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false I would have seen one of: (a) a single shared helper — RecalcUnit delegating to custom.EncodeTimerDuration or a common constant, i.e. one declaration of 16343 rather than two in different packages; (b) Timer.SetDuration converting its float64 to an integer before SetValue; or (c) a coercion on the write path — CheckAgainstPD true, or parameter.Coerce called inside ValueWriter — which would have made both paths produce the identical wire integer. I looked for each and found none.
stands.reason: Both copies are live and address the same DURATION_VALUE / DURATION_UNIT pair on the same siren channel, and their outputs differ in type and in value. The threshold 16343 is declared twice in two packages with no link between them, so a firmware-driven correction to one leaves the other on the old bucket boundary. Severity is medium rather than high: for an integral duration <= 16343 s (the common case) both paths yield the same number, and the divergence is confined to the MQTT combined-write path. What the CCU does when it receives a <double> for a parameter declared INTEGER is a firmware question I cannot answer read-only — unverified. Note additionally that the doc comment at projection.go:107-109, "fractional values are honoured because the wire unit promotion works on the seconds total, not on integers", is contradicted by mixins.go:215 "DURATION_VALUE is an INTEGER parameter".
stands.divergence: Concrete: a combined MQTT write of "16373" to a siren's DURATION. WriteCombined -> SetDuration -> RecalcUnit(16373) returns (272.8833333333333, TimerUnitMinutes) and stages the float64 272.8833333333333 on DURATION_VALUE. The same 16373 s requested through Siren.TurnOn -> custom.EncodeTimerDuration(16373*time.Second) returns (int32(272), 1). Reachable at an ordinary duration too: WriteCombined("1.5") -> RecalcUnit(1.5) = (1.5, Seconds) -> float64 1.5 on the INTEGER DURATION_VALUE, where EncodeTimerDuration(1.5s) returns (1, 0).
stands.deadCopy: Neither. Both have production callers (siren.go:328 etc. for EncodeTimerDuration; mqtt_sink.go:470 -> projection.go:118 -> timer.go:250 for RecalcUnit).
stands.guard: None comparing them. combined_test.go:178 TestTimerRecalcUnitThresholds and custom_test.go:261 TestEncodeTimerDurationTruncatesTowardZero pin the two separately; both stay green while the two drift apart.
stands.secondReason: Survived every bite. The quotes are current; the two functions encode the same rule for the same two wire parameters on the same channel with no import barrier between them (combined already imports custom for TimerNotUsed); both have production callers; the divergent input sits inside the range the HA number entity itself advertises; and the coercion that would have erased the divergence does not exist anywhere between Timer.SetDuration and the XML-RPC encoder. by_design.md:4319 makes the intended rule explicit - promote in float, truncate at the write boundary because DURATION_VALUE is INTEGER - and the combined path ports only the first half. Severity stays medium rather than high for one honest reason: what CCU firmware does with a <double> on a parameter declared INTEGER cannot be answered read-only, so the observable-damage leg is unverified in those words. A live write showing the firmware rejecting or mis-scaling the double would make this high.

stands.title: The whole Homematic value-conversion rule set exists twice; the model copy has no production caller
stands.evidence: Both quotes are accurate. internal/model/value/converter.go:61-62 'case float64:\n\t\treturn roundFloat(val, 6)' vs internal/parameter/converter.go:55-56 'case float64:\n\t\treturn math.Round(v*1_000_000) / 1_000_000'. internal/model/value/converter.go:33 'var ConvertableParameters = [...]hmenum.Parameter{' vs internal/parameter/converter.go:19 'var ConvertableParameters = map[hmenum.Parameter]struct{}{'. The rule-set overlap is real: bool->1/0, float32/float64 six-decimal rounding, time.Duration->Seconds(), time.Time->RFC3339, the bool/time coercion in FromHomematicValue, and the two-entry convertable set are each written out twice. Import grep: `grep -rn "internal/model/value" --include="*.go" .` returns ONLY tests/contract/convertable_parameter_parity_test.go:9, internal/model/value/converter_test.go:11 and internal/model/value/converter_extra_test.go:10 - the whole package has no production importer. `grep -rn "ToHomematicValue|FromHomematicValue" | grep -v _test.go` returns only the two declaration files plus internal/parameter/converter.go:66,72 (its own recursion): NEITHER copy of the conversion functions has a production caller. What IS live from internal/parameter is only the predicate and the encoder: internal/client/interface_client_orchestration.go:324 'if paramconvert.IsConvertable(parameter) {' (alias declared at :27) and internal/model/custom/cover/blind.go:346 'parameter.ConvertHMLevelToCPV(...)'.
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false I would have seen either (a) a non-test file importing internal/model/value, or (b) the two implementations agreeing on nil / fmt.Stringer / []any / int64, i.e. the same result for the diverging inputs below. Both greps returned production hits for internal/parameter's IsConvertable and ConvertHMLevelToCPV in the same run, so the grep was not silently broken.
stands.divergence: ToHomematicValue([]any{true}): internal/parameter returns []any{1} (recursion arm, converter.go:63-68); internal/model/value returns []any{true} unchanged (no []any arm, falls through to 'return v' at converter.go:70). ToHomematicValue(hmenum.InterfaceHmIPRF) (a fmt.Stringer, the exact input internal/parameter/converter_test.go:60 uses): internal/parameter returns the string "HmIP-RF" (converter.go:73-74); internal/model/value returns the hmenum.Interface value unchanged. Opposite direction: FromHomematicValue(int64(1), "bool"): internal/model/value returns true (converter.go:87-88 'case int64: return val != 0'); internal/parameter returns int64(1) with a nil error (its bool switch has int/float64/bool arms only, converter.go:91-99, default returns the value). So each copy handles a case the other drops.
stands.deadCopy: Both ToHomematicValue/FromHomematicValue copies are dead. internal/model/value is dead as a whole package (no production importer). internal/parameter's ConvertableParameters/IsConvertable IS live (interface_client_orchestration.go:324); internal/model/value's mirror of that set is not.
stands.guard: tests/contract/convertable_parameter_parity_test.go (TestConvertableParameterSetsAgree) pins only set membership and size - its comment at :17-21 even asserts the model side is a live 'model-side mirror'. No test compares ToHomematicValue/FromHomematicValue outputs across the two packages, so the four divergences above are unguarded.
stands.reason: Duplication confirmed and quotes accurate, but the candidate's damage sentence is wrong in one respect: it says 'Every non-test reference in the tree is to internal/parameter'. For the conversion functions there is no non-test reference at all - internal/parameter.ToHomematicValue is equally uncalled. So nothing writes an unconverted paramset today; the live write path (interface_client_orchestration.go:324) only asks IsConvertable. What is real: an entire test-only package whose doc comment ('Package value provides converters between Go-native types and Homematic wire values') advertises itself as the conversion home, with four behavioural gaps against the sibling, guarded only on the parameter set. Severity medium rather than high: no live path drifts today, but the dead copy is the weaker one and it is the one a reader is invited to reach for.
stands.secondReason: Survived all five bites. Quote: accurate, lines current. Sameness: not two readings of one datum -- both doc comments cite the same reference `to_homematic` singledispatch and both enumerate the same rule list, so this is one rule set written twice; the differing signature (`any` vs `(any, error)`) is a shape difference, not a purpose difference. Liveness: the copy is deader than claimed -- the whole package, not just the converter pair, has zero production importers. Divergence: reproduced by reading both paths, five gaps not four (see divergence field). Damage: this is the bite that partly lands, and it is why I downgrade medium -> low. Neither copy is production-reachable, so no shipping behaviour can change and no drift is observable today; the harm is a test-only package whose doc comment at :4-6 advertises itself as 'converters between Go-native types and Homematic wire values', which is the copy a future contributor reaches for, and it is the weaker one -- it silently drops []any, map[string]any and fmt.Stringer, and its own comment promises the fmt.Stringer arm it lacks. Confirmed as dead code plus a false doc claim plus a guard resting on a false rationale, not as a drift risk.

stands.title: Channel-group membership is stored twice with opposite tie-breaks: first-wins on the channel, last-wins on the device
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false I would have seen one of two things: (a) an existence guard on internal/model/device/aggregate.go:360 in the shape of the one at :363, making both copies first-wins — the guard is present two lines below and absent on the channelNo write; or (b) `grep -rn "GetChannelGroupNo\|IsInMultiChannelGroup" --include="*.go" .` returning a caller outside a _test.go file — it returns only the two definitions in aggregate.go plus their own tests. Neither appeared.
stands.divergence:
Device model HmIP-WGT (registered four times in internal/model/custom/profiles.go:1359-1398 with DeviceType "hmip-wgt": IPThermostat@8, IPDimmer@2, IPButtonLock@0, IPSwitch@4). IPDimmer's config (internal/model/custom/profile_configs.go:109-116) has PrimaryChannel 0, StateChannelOffset -1, SecondaryChannels [1,2] -> base 2 claims channels 1,2,3,4 for group 2. IPSwitch's config (:420-427) is identical in shape -> base 4 claims channels 3,4,5,6 for group 4. Category sort puts "light" before "switch", so IPDimmer writes first.
Result for channel 4 (and identically for channel 3):
  Channel.GroupNumber() == 2   (first-wins, kept from IPDimmer)
  Device.GetChannelGroupNo(4) == 4   (last-wins, overwritten by IPSwitch)
And Device.GroupChannels reports channel 4 as a member of both group 2 ([1 2 3 4]) and group 4 ([3 4 5 6]).
stands.deadCopy: Site B. The reverse map internal/model/device/aggregate.go:162 `channelToGroup` is read only by Device.GetChannelGroupNo (aggregate.go:424-427) and Device.IsInMultiChannelGroup (:432-433), and neither has a production caller — grep excluding _test.go returns only the definitions. The two tests that pin them (internal/model/device/device_test.go:598 TestGetChannelGroupNoKnownChannel, internal/model/device/channel_parameter_accessor_test.go:285 TestDeviceIsInMultiChannelGroup) stay green on the last-wins answer while every live consumer reads the first-wins one: internal/model/device/channel_payload.go:49, internal/model/device/channel.go:892 (IsInMultiGroup), :956 (GroupMaster), internal/model/custom/schedule_targets.go:64, internal/model/custom/materialize.go:194, internal/north/rest/handlers/devices.go:750 and internal/north/mqtt/discovery.go:1407 all call Channel.GroupNumber(); Device.HasSubDevices (aggregate.go:496-511) reads only the forward map's member counts.
stands.guard: none — no test compares Channel.GroupNumber() against Device.GetChannelGroupNo() for the same channel. internal/model/custom/materialize_group_publication_test.go is the only materialiser-side group test and it asserts Channel.GroupNumber() alone (:100-102) on a single-profile fixture.
stands.reason:
Both quotes are accurate and both writes are issued unconditionally from one function, so the two stores of the same fact really do apply opposite tie-breaks, with a concrete device (HmIP-WGT, channels 3 and 4) where they already return different answers today. I lower the severity from high to medium because the candidate's damage claim is not borne out: every live consumer named in it (MQTT sub-device discovery, HasSubDevices, schedule targets, channel_payload group_no/is_group_master, Room/GroupMaster fallback) reads Channel.GroupNumber() or the forward groupChannels map, never the diverging reverse map. What is real is the dead-copy trap — two exported Device methods that answer the same question the wrong way and are pinned by passing tests, so the first production caller to reach for the convenient device-level lookup silently re-points the sub-device split.
One further observed fact, offered as an unverified-impact note rather than a finding: the forward map genuinely lists channels 3 and 4 under both group 2 and group 4, which is what makes HmIP-WGT satisfy HasSubDevices' "at least two groups with more than one member" test. I did not trace whether that is intended for this device.
stands.secondReason:
Survives on the quote, the sameness and the divergence; the auditor's own downgrade to medium is the right calibration, and I confirmed the liveness argument behind it.

Sameness holds: these are not two readings of one datum for two callers. Both maps answer the identical question "which group does channel N belong to", both are written from the same call site in the same loop iteration, and aggregate.go:338-341 says so outright — "The Channel itself already carries its own group number ([Channel.GroupNumber]); this map exists so coordinators can resolve 'give me every channel of group N' cheaply." The stated justification covers the forward map only; the reverse map at :360 is a third store that the comment does not account for.

Damage today is nil, and the reverse map is deader than the auditor claimed. grep over the whole tree: Device.GetChannelGroupNo (aggregate.go:424) has no production caller — only internal/model/device/device_test.go:598-613 and its own wrapper Device.IsInMultiChannelGroup (aggregate.go:432), which has zero callers anywhere, tests included. Every live consumer reads the other side: MQTT sub-device discovery via discovery.go:1407 sdi.GroupNumber(); REST devices.go:750 ch.GroupNumber(); channel_payload.go:49; schedule targets custom/schedule_targets.go:64; materialize.go:194; Channel.IsInMultiGroup (channel.go:892-896) and HasSubDevices (aggregate.go:496-511) both read d.groupChannels, the forward map.

That is what makes it worth a backlog entry rather than a hazard: two exported Device methods, pinned green by tests, that answer a question the wrong way for a device already in the catalogue. The first production caller that reaches for the convenient device-level lookup silently re-points the sub-device split, and the test suite will not notice.

One correction to the auditor's unverified-impact note: HasSubDevices does not depend on the diverging map at all. aggregate.go:499-510 counts groups in d.groupChannels with more than one member; the HmIP-WGT overlap makes both group 2 and group 4 multi-member, so the device does split. Whether that split is intended for HmIP-WGT is a separate question the source does not answer — I did not trace it either.

stands.title: The press-parameter family is enumerated five times inside internal/model/generic
stands.evidence:
Quotes verified verbatim. button.go:414-419 `func isPressParameter(p hmenum.Parameter) bool {\n\tswitch p {\n\tcase hmenum.ParameterPress, hmenum.ParameterPressShort,\n\t\themenum.ParameterPressLong, hmenum.ParameterPressLongStart,\n\t\themenum.ParameterPressLongRelease, hmenum.ParameterPressCont:`. The identical six-case list is repeated at action.go:59-64 (`func (a *Action) MatterMeasurementClass()` … `return interfaces.MatterMeasurementMomentarySwitch`) and matter.go:77-80 (inside `matterMeasurementForParameter`). The four-case long-press subset is repeated at button.go:427-431 (`func isLongPressParameter`) and action.go:75-79 (`func (a *Action) MatterSwitchSupportsLongPress`). Five enumerations, as claimed.

The coupling is real and the code says so: internal/north/matter/endpoint/assembler.go:534 collects a DP into `pressMembers` when `meas.MatterMeasurementClass() == interfaces.MatterMeasurementMomentarySwitch` (the action.go / matter.go lists), and assembler.go:692 hands that slice to `generic.NewButtonGroup`, whose member filter is `if !isPressParameter(p) { continue }` (button.go:167 — the button.go list). assembler.go:677-680 states the assumption in prose: `// Returns (nil, nil) when no member survives the group's press-family filter —\n// defensive only, since the MomentarySwitch classification and the\n// group's press family enumerate the same parameters.` Nothing enforces that.

Liveness: isPressParameter/isLongPressParameter are called from production at button.go:53, :70, :167, :171 (grep excludes the same-named `isPressParameter(p string)` in internal/north/mqtt/discovery_aggregate.go:28, a different function on a different type). Action's copies are reachable: internal/central/adapter/datapoint_resolver.go:164-171 builds a `generic.Action` for a write-only ACTION parameter that is not in `buttonActionParameters` (only RESET_MOTION / RESET_PRESENCE, datapoint_resolver.go:90-93) and has no VALUE_LIST.

Note: hmenum.ClickEvents (pkg/hmenum/parameter.go:200-209) and internal/model/event/event.go:287-296 hold an eight-member superset including PRESS_LOCK / PRESS_UNLOCK. That is a deliberate divergence, documented at button.go:410-413, not a sixth copy of the same set.
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false I would have found either a single shared helper referenced by all five sites, or a test enumerating the family once and asserting the other sites against it. Neither exists: `grep -rn "isPressParameter" --include="*_test.go"` returns nothing, and the two tests that do enumerate the family — internal/model/generic/matter_test.go:113 and internal/model/generic/button_action_matter_test.go:611-615 — each hard-code their own literal list, so each would stay green while the other site drifted.
stands.reason: Structural claim verified in full: five independent enumerations, no shared source, no guard. Severity reduced from the candidate's `high` to `medium` because (a) all three six-case lists and both four-case subsets are set-identical today — I compared them member by member and found no diverging input, so this is drift risk, not a live defect; (b) the primary failure mode is fail-closed: a member classified MomentarySwitch but rejected by isPressParameter leaves `pressMembers` non-empty while `NewButtonGroup` returns nil (button.go:177-179), so makeButtonGroupEndpoint returns (nil, nil) and the button silently gets no endpoint at all. The wrong-advertisement direction the candidate names (long-press advertised without emission) is real but needs the two four-case subsets to diverge.
stands.divergence: None. All three six-case lists contain exactly {Press, PressShort, PressLong, PressLongStart, PressLongRelease, PressCont}; both four-case lists contain exactly {PressLong, PressLongStart, PressLongRelease, PressCont}. No input separates them today.
stands.deadCopy: internal/model/generic/matter.go:77-80 — the press arm of matterMeasurementForParameter is unreachable in production. Its only callers are matter.go:128 (Sensor[T].MatterMeasurementClass) and matter.go:142 (BinarySensor.MatterMeasurementClass), and no PRESS_* parameter can become a Sensor or BinarySensor: every one of them is in hmenum.ClickEvents (pkg/hmenum/parameter.go:200-209), and internal/central/adapter/datapoint_resolver.go:181-188 returns `generic.NewButton(...)` on `if param.IsClickEvent()` before reaching the isBinarySensor / TYPE switch at :189-199. The only other production constructors of these types (internal/model/calculated/climate.go:504, derived_binary.go:291) use synthetic parameter names. The arm is exercised solely by internal/model/generic/matter_test.go:111-118.
stands.guard: None.
stands.secondReason: Survives every attack I ran. (1) Sameness: these are not one datum read two ways — Button proves it, since button.go:53 (`if isPressParameter(hmenum.Parameter(b.Key.Parameter))` inside MatterMeasurementClass) and button.go:70 (`return isLongPressParameter(...)`) call the helpers from exactly the method shapes Action re-inlines at action.go:59 and :75. The type system does not force the repetition. (2) Liveness of the load-bearing pair: isPressParameter gates ButtonGroup membership (button.go:167-179) and NewButtonGroup is called from production at internal/north/matter/endpoint/assembler.go:692; Action.MatterMeasurementClass is the gate that defers a press DP into pressMembers (assembler.go:534-540). Those two must agree. (3) Damage: they can drift and the drift is observable — a member classified MomentarySwitch (action.go:59) but rejected by isPressParameter leaves pressMembers non-empty while NewButtonGroup returns nil (button.go:177-179), so makeButtonGroupEndpoint returns (nil, nil) (assembler.go:693-695) and the button gets no GenericSwitch endpoint at all. Severity stays medium, not high: the sets are identical today, so this is drift risk, not a live defect.

stands.title: The electrical-parameter set is defined twice, and the comment pinning them names a function and a test that do not exist
stands.evidence:
Comment verified verbatim at internal/model/generic/electrical.go:51-54: `// Kept in lock-step with the Power/Energy arms of
// matterMeasurementForAnalogParameter: a parameter classified electrical there
// but missing here would be collected into the group and then silently dropped.
// TestElectricalGroupCoversEveryElectricalParameter pins the two together.`

Both named identifiers are fictional. `grep -rn "matterMeasurementForAnalogParameter" --include="*.go" .` returns exactly one line: internal/model/generic/electrical.go:52 (the comment itself). The real function is `matterMeasurementForParameter`, internal/model/generic/matter.go:40. `grep -rn "TestElectricalGroupCoversEveryElectricalParameter" -r .` likewise returns only internal/model/generic/electrical.go:54. The tests that do exist in internal/model/generic/electrical_test.go are TestElectricalGroupRoutesEachParameterToItsOwnSlot, …UnpopulatedSlotReportsNoObservation, …HasEnergyIsAboutTheSourceNotTheReading, …PrefersConsumptionOverFeedIn, …IgnoresNonElectricalMembers, …NilCases, …FansOutChangeNotifications, …NilCallbackIsIgnored — none of them reads matterMeasurementForParameter.

The two lists are genuinely independent. electrical.go:55-70 `func electricalParameterSlot(p hmenum.Parameter) (slot string, ok bool) { switch p { case hmenum.ParameterPower: return "activePower", true; case hmenum.ParameterVoltage: return "voltage", true; case hmenum.ParameterCurrent: return "current", true; case hmenum.ParameterFrequency: return "frequency", true; case hmenum.ParameterEnergyCounter, hmenum.ParameterEnergyCounterFeedIn: return "energy", true` versus matter.go:71-75 `case hmenum.ParameterPower, hmenum.ParameterCurrent,
		hemenum.ParameterVoltage, hmenum.ParameterFrequency:
		return interfaces.MatterMeasurementPower
	case hmenum.ParameterEnergyCounter, hmenum.ParameterEnergyCounterFeedIn:

stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false I would have seen either (a) one set derived from the other (e.g. edgeTriggerParameters built by cloning ClickEvents and adding the two CODE_* entries), or (b) the eight entries differing between the two literals, or (c) one of the two sets with no non-test caller. The knowledge is genuinely shared: edgeTriggerParameters is a strict superset that could be expressed as ClickEvents plus {CODE_ID, CODE_STATE} but is not. Severity medium rather than low because the failure is silent and safety-adjacent: a press parameter added to ClickEvents alone is deduplicated away at event.go:205 and the alarm intent router never sees the repeat. Probability is bounded by the fact that the eight PRESS_* names are a fixed CCU firmware vocabulary.
stands.divergence: None found. The eight press entries are byte-identical in both literals. stands.guard: None. stands.deadCopy: Neither. Both sets have multiple non-test callers (listed in evidence).
stands.secondReason: Survived every bite. The quote is verbatim and the line numbers are current. Both literals are live with four distinct production consumers each, serving genuinely different layers (DP shape / visibility vs. dedup / persistence) — so this is not an EnumLabel-vs-EnumLabelFromWire pair where each reading is right for its caller; it is one datum (which eight names are momentary button pushes) transcribed twice. stands.title: LIKE wildcards are escaped for the audit device filter and never for the device-prefix deletes or the energy read path
stands.evidence:
audit.go:190 verbatim: `func escapeLikePrefix(s string) string {` / :191 `return strings.NewReplacer(`\`, `\\`, `%`, `\%`, `_`, `\_`).Replace(s)` — the candidate cited :188, which is the first comment line; the func is at :190. Paired at audit.go:155 `where = append(where, `device_address LIKE ? ESCAPE '\'`)` / :156 `args = append(args, escapeLikePrefix(q.Device)+"%")`.
measurements.go:1877-1880 verbatim: `deleteDeviceRawSQL = `\n `DELETE FROM measurements`\n ` WHERE central_name = ? AND interface_id = ?`\n ` AND (channel_address = ? OR channel_address LIKE ? || '%' ESCAPE '\')`` — bound at :1858-1860 with the raw `prefix` from :1844. Identical shape in master_values.go:189-191, values_cache.go:435-438, paramsets.go:312-315, channel_flags.go:120-123, recording_overrides.go:125-129: every one declares ESCAPE '\' and binds an unescaped address.
Worse than the candidate states, the energy read path declares no ESCAPE at all: measurements.go:1095 and :1105 `AND (? = '' OR channel_address = ? OR channel_address LIKE ?)` bound at :1218-1220 / :1235-1237 with `prefix := deviceAddr + ":%"`.
No validation upstream of either: internal/north/rest/handlers/energy.go:147 `Device: v.Get("device")` (parseEnergyQuery checks only that `central` is non-empty, :149-151), and internal/central/cachereset/cachereset.go:63-65 `if s.Central == "" || s.Interface == "" || s.Device == "" {` is the whole of Scope.Validate for a device scope. `grep -rn "IsDeviceAddress" internal/north` returns nothing. pkg/hmtypes/address.go:24 `var deviceAddressPattern = regexp.MustCompile(`^[0-9a-zA-Z-]{5,20}$`)` exists but is never consulted on either path.
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false, the DELETE binds would read `escapeLikePrefix(prefix)` the way audit.go:156 does, or a validator would reject a wildcard before the store. I grepped for escapeLikePrefix across the package: it appears only at audit.go:156 and its own definition at :190 — no other call site. And Scope.Validate / parseEnergyQuery would have shown a format check; both check only emptiness.
stands.reason: Confirmed, and the reachability the candidate flagged as unknown is answered by the code rather than by firmware: the pattern is not built from a CCU-supplied address on either path I checked — it is built from an unvalidated HTTP parameter. Whether a real CCU address can contain '_' is therefore not the load-bearing question; the store accepts any string. Severity kept at medium: the destructive path (POST /api/v1/admin/cache/clear) is admin-gated and clears a cache that is re-pulled from the CCU by design, so nothing is permanently lost; the read path returns wrong data rather than losing it.
stands.divergence: device = "%" (single percent sign). Audit filter (audit.go:155-156): escaped to `\%` → matches only a device literally named "%" → 0 rows. Cache clear with Scope{Kind:"device", Device:"%"} (passes Validate at cachereset.go:63, reaches cachereset.go:329/337/349): prefix "%:" → `LIKE '%:' || '%'` = `'%:%'` → matches every channel address → deletes every paramset, cached VALUES and cached MASTER row for that (central, interface). Energy read `GET /api/v1/energy?central=X&device=%25`: prefix "%:%" → `channel_address LIKE '%:%'` with no ESCAPE → every channel of every device is returned under the one requested device. Second input, `device = "A_C123"`: audit matches only "A_C123…"; the deletes match "AXC123:0" as well, because '_' is a single-character wildcard.

stands.guard: None. stands.secondReason: The quote is current, the asymmetry is real, and the reachability the candidate flagged as unknown is answered by the code, not by firmware: on both paths the LIKE pattern is built from an unvalidated HTTP parameter, so whether a genuine CCU address can contain '%' or '_' is not load-bearing. I attacked the sameness (audit's filter is a user-typed search prefix, the deletes take an identifier — arguably two rules) and it does not save the finding: the identifier is not validated anywhere either, so the deletes are handling untrusted text with the escape clause declared and the escaping omitted. stands.title: The weighted-versus-legacy degrade rule is implemented four times — three in Go, once in SQL — with no test on the mixed merge

:919 (foldTierBuckets, declared :885) `if a.weightMs == 0 || b.weightMs == 0 {`, preceded by :917-918 `// See [foldTierBucketsBy]: a mix of a spanned and an unspanned` / `// source row degrades the merged bucket to the legacy pair.`
:1405 (foldEnergyRowsBy, declared :1375) `if a.row.weightMs == 0 || r.weightMs == 0 {` / :1406 `a.row.weightedSum, a.row.weightMs = 0, 0`
:1664 (rollupDailySelectSQL, declared :1648) `CASE WHEN MIN(weight_ms) OVER w = 0 THEN 0 ELSE SUM(weighted_sum) OVER w END,` / :1665 the same for weight_ms.
All four live: foldTierBucketsBy ← measurements.go:771; foldTierBuckets ← measurements.go:392; foldEnergyRowsBy ← measurements.go:1301 and :1357; rollupDailySelectSQL ← measurements.go:1766 inside RollupDaily (:1691), called from internal/history/recorder.go:485.

And had a guard existed, a test would drive one spanned and one unspanned row into the same output bucket; `grep -n "insertHourlyRowWeighted("` across all of internal/store/sqlite returns exactly two lines — the helper's own definition at measurements_weighted_rollup_columns_test.go:17 and one call at :165 — so no test ever inserts two rows with differing weight_ms.
stands.reason: Confirmed as a four-way duplication of a rule whose partial application is silently wrong, with all four copies live and no guard. The copies agree today: the SQL's partition-wide `MIN(weight_ms) OVER w = 0` and the Go pairwise zeroing produce the same result, because once a Go accumulator is zeroed it stays zeroed. Severity medium rather than high: no divergence exists yet, so nothing is wrong in the shipped output; the exposure is that a fifth fold, or an edit to one of the four, would silently report a time-weighted mean over only the hours whose span it knows, in the user-facing energy and history charts, and nothing would go red.
stands.divergence: None today — I looked for one and did not find it. The closest is TestMeasurement_QueryBuckets_LegacyRollupRowFallsBackToSampleMean (internal/store/sqlite/measurements_weighted_rollup_columns_test.go:149), which inserts a single all-legacy row (weighted_sum=0, weight_ms=0 at :168) and asserts the sample mean comes back. stands.title: The SQLite busy timeout is stated as five unrelated literals
stands.evidence:
All three quoted sites verified verbatim, plus two more the candidate missed.
dsn.go:28 `const connectionPragmas = "_pragma=busy_timeout(5000)&_pragma=journal_mode(WAL)&_pragma=foreign_keys(1)" +`
store.go:130 `"PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000",` inside applyPragmas
health_probe.go:45 `const sqliteBusyTimeout = 5 * time.Second`, with the coupling asserted in prose at :38-44: `// sqliteBusyTimeout mirrors the `busy_timeout` pragma every pooled` / `// connection carries (dsn.go's connectionPragmas, applyPragmas in` / `// store.go): SQLite itself will hold a writer-blocked query open for up to` / `// this long before returning SQLITE_BUSY, so the probe's own deadline below` / `// must clear it — otherwise a lock wait the database is configured to` / `// tolerate gets reported as a probe failure before SQLite ever gives up on` / `// it.`
Not cited by the candidate: store.go:189 `db, err := sql.Open(DriverName, "file:"+path+"?mode=ro&_pragma=busy_timeout(5000)")` and cmd/openccu-loom/backup.go:475 `const busyTimeout = "_pragma=busy_timeout(5000)"`.
The consumption the damage claim rests on is real: health_probe.go:102 `queryCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, sqliteBusyTimeout+degradedLatencyBudget)`, and the error branch at :110-114 documents `// this trips ServiceAvailability/HTTP 503 immediately via the second Record below, which escalates DEGRADED to UNHEALTHY.` All sites are live: FileDSN is the daemon's only file-open path (daemon_boot.go:112 and the five *_wiring.go files), applyPragmas runs from Open (store.go:65), StartHealthProbe is the probe wired into the daemon's health tracker, store.go:189 is the read-only open, backup.go:475 the backup tool's.
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false, one exported constant would be referenced by every site and `grep -rn "busy_timeout|busyTimeout"` would return one definition plus references. It returns five independent literals in four files (plus one unrelated 2000 in tests/integration/admin_e2e_test.go:65). Had a guard existed, a test would assert the probe constant against the DSN string; the same grep returns no assertion in any _test.go — only health_probe_test.go's latency-budget helpers, which touch healthyLatencyBudget/degradedLatencyBudget and never sqliteBusyTimeout.
stands.reason: Confirmed: one value, five statements, no shared source and no guard, with a comment at health_probe.go:38-44 that asserts the coupling it cannot enforce (per the project's own rule, a comment naming a relationship is a hypothesis, not a check). Severity medium — nothing is wrong today, but the drift is one-directional and its failure is loud: raise the pragma without raising health_probe.go:45 and the probe's 5.5 s deadline expires while SQLite is still legitimately waiting on a writer lock, err != nil, the store component escalates to UNHEALTHY and /health returns 503 on a database that is working as configured. That is precisely the outcome the constant's comment says it exists to prevent.
stands.divergence: None today — all five sites are 5000 ms / 5 s. This is a drift-risk finding, not a present disagreement; I looked for a diverging value and found none.
stands.deadCopy: None — all five sites have production callers.
stands.guard: None. No test asserts sqliteBusyTimeout against connectionPragmas or against the applyPragmas literal.
stands.secondReason: Every quote is current and the coupling is real and one-directional, so I cannot kill it — but the title overstates and I downgrade medium to low. Two of the five are not copies of the pooled rule at all: store.go:189 (SchemaVersionOfFile) and backup.go:475 (openForVacuum) are one-shot read-only opens of an archived or being-backed-up file, whose lock tolerance is an independent knob that need not track the daemon pool's pragma — sharing a value today is not the same as sharing a rule. The load-bearing set is three: dsn.go:28 (the pool DSN, the value that actually governs every connection), store.go:130 (applyPragmas, which by its own file's comment at :118-125 primes only the single connection sql.DB hands ExecContext), and health_probe.go:45. Of those, the one coupling whose breach is silent already carries a prose comment naming it — which is exactly the project's "a comment naming a relationship is a hypothesis, not a check" rule, so a guard asserting `sqliteBusyTimeout == the value parsed out of connectionPragmas` is the cheap close. No present defect: all five read 5000 ms / 5 s.

stands.title: The backup ceiling is calibrated against a backend poll budget that does not exist
stands.evidence:
Quotes verified verbatim. stubs.go:39-42: `// backupRunTimeout bounds the detached create-and-download goroutine. It` / `// sits above the backend's own 300 s poll budget so the backend reports a` / `// clean timeout before this hard ceiling cancels the context.` / `const backupRunTimeout = 6 * time.Minute`. It is live: stubs.go:256 `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), backupRunTimeout)` inside runBackup, reached from TriggerBackup (stubs.go:167/185), routed at internal/north/rest/router.go:1239.

The backend side says the opposite of the adapter comment, in its own doc: ccu_extended.go:620-625 `// A positive maxWaitTime bounds the whole exchange in seconds; zero or` / `// negative leaves the bound to the caller's context and the HTTP client,` / `// which is what every production caller wants — its own deadline is the` / `// budget for the backup, and a second, shorter one here would abort a run` / `// the caller still had time for.` and ccu_extended.go:647 `if maxWaitTime > 0 {` — the only place a timeout is applied.

The production caller passes 0: hub_wiring.go:2736 `return ic.CreateBackupAndDownload(ctx, b, 0, 0)`, live via ccu_wiring.go:561 `WireBackupAndDownload(unit, writer)` → central.go:998 SetCreateBackupFn → central.go:987 Unit.CreateBackup, which stubs.go:275 calls (`data, err := u.CreateBackup(ctx)`).

The cited 300 s budget exists nowhere: `grep -rn "300" --include="*.go" internal/client/backends/ | grep -v test` returns nothing at all. The only two occurrences of the number in this area are the two comments themselves — stubs.go:40 and hub_wiring.go:2726 `// poll parameters selects the backend defaults (300 s wait, 5 s interval).`

One sub-claim in the candidate is wrong and I correct it: firmwareDownloadTimeout (ccu.go:23, 10 min) is NOT the production client. ccu_extended.go:680-682 uses it only as a nil-fallback (`hc := b.httpClient` / `if hc == nil { hc = httpx.NewClient(firmwareDownloadTimeout) }`), and production always wires a non-nil client at ccu_wiring.go:885 `ccuBackend.SetDownloadFirmwareTransport(ccuBaseURLFor(cc), hc, sessionIDFn)` with hc from hub_wiring.go:828 jsonrpcHTTPClient(cc) — which returns nil unless TLS+InsecureSkipVerify, in which case ccu_wiring.go:864 substitutes `&http.Client{Transport: httpx.NewTransport()}` with the comment `// No timeout here by design`. So in the default configuration the HTTP client has NO timeout at all and backupRunTimeout is the only bound; with TLS+insecure it is 30 s (jsonrpcHTTPClient). Neither is 300 s, and the correction makes the finding stronger, not weaker.
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false, the backends tree would carry a default such as `const backupMaxWaitSeconds = 300` or `if maxWaitTime <= 0 { maxWaitTime = 300 }` inside CreateBackupAndDownload, and the grep for "300" under internal/client/backends/ would have returned it. It returned zero non-test lines, and the function's own doc comment explicitly disclaims any internal default for maxWaitTime <= 0.
stands.reason: Both sites are live production code and they already contradict each other in prose: the adapter comment asserts a backend budget that the backend's own doc comment explicitly says does not exist. No functional bug is provable today (6 min does bound the run, and a CCU backup normally completes in well under that), but the documented failure ordering is inverted — a slow backup is killed by the adapter's context, surfacing as `backup.create.failed` with a context error rather than the promised clean backend timeout. Medium: the same false budget is asserted twice (stubs.go:40, hub_wiring.go:2726), so a future maintainer sizing the ceiling reads a phantom constraint from two independent places.
stands.divergence: No input where two code paths return different values — this is a prose/behaviour divergence, not a value divergence. Concrete case where the documented ordering fails: a CCU whose backup archive takes >6 min to build (default config, no TLS-insecure, so the HTTP client has no timeout). The backend has no deadline of its own and the goroutine's ctx expires at 6 min → operator sees a context-cancellation error, not the "clean timeout" the comment promises.

stands.evidence:
Quotes verified verbatim. health_wiring.go:119-124: `case hmenum.ClientStateFailed,` / `hmenum.ClientStateStopped:` / `record(e.InterfaceID, false, fmt.Sprintf("client %s", e.To))` / `// Hit the same component a second time so the tracker escalates DEGRADED` / `// → UNHEALTHY immediately.` / `record(e.InterfaceID, false, fmt.Sprintf("client %s (escalated)", e.To))`. Repeated at :139-140 (`record(e.InterfaceID, false, "breaker open")` / `record(e.InterfaceID, false, "breaker open (escalated)")`) and :159-160 (`record(e.InterfaceID, false, fmt.Sprintf("recovery failed: %s (attempts=%d)", e.Reason, e.Attempts))` / `record(e.InterfaceID, false, "recovery failed (escalated)")`).

The owning threshold is at internal/health/tracker.go:221-225: `// Flap-damp: a single unhealthy sample after a healthy run yields` / `// DEGRADED; two consecutive unhealthy samples escalate to UNHEALTHY.` / `if known && !sample.Healthy && prev.Status == StatusHealthy {` / `status = StatusDegraded` / `}`.

The candidate undercounts: the same threshold is encoded at FIVE production sites, not three. internal/north/mqtt/health_probe.go:86-94 `// Disconnected — escalate to UNHEALTHY immediately via the` / `// double-sample flap-damp rule.` … `tracker.Record(HealthComponentName, health.Sample{Healthy: false, Note: "disconnected (escalated)"})`; internal/north/matter/bridge/health_probe.go:93-101 `// Listener gone. Escalate immediately via the double-sample` / `// flap-damp rule — matches the MQTT-disconnected handling.` … `Note: "bridge listener not bound (escalated)"`.

The i18n leakage claim is verified too: health_wiring.go:28 `"breaker open (escalated)": "health.note.breaker_open_escalated",` and :31 `"recovery failed (escalated)": "health.note.recovery_failed_escalated",` in healthNoteKeys, resolving to internal/i18n/catalogs/en.json:69 and :74 and to assets/ui/src/lib/i18n.ts:983/986 (en) and :4864/4867 (de). Those two catalogue entries exist only because a numeric threshold is expressed as a second, differently-worded sample.

I checked whether the tracker offers an escalate-now API that the wiring is working around: it does not. The full method list on *Tracker (tracker.go:191-1138) has Record and RecordQuality only, and RecordQuality is capped — tracker.go:255 `// CAPPED at [StatusDegraded] — a quality signal must never escalate a component`. So there is no non-duplicating way to express "unhealthy now" today.
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false, health_wiring would call record once per incident and the tracker would expose a direct immediate-unhealthy entry point (a Force flag on Sample, or a RecordUnhealthy method). I enumerated every *Tracker method (`grep -n "^func (t \*Tracker)" internal/health/tracker.go`, 42 methods) and found no such entry point, and both the wiring comments and the mqtt/matter comments name the double-sample rule explicitly as the mechanism they are exploiting. A false claim would also have shown a de-duplication guard inside Record; Record at tracker.go:227-231 appends every sample unconditionally.
stands.reason: A numeric threshold that belongs to internal/health.Tracker is re-encoded as a call-pattern at five production sites, plus two invented display strings that had to be carried into both i18n catalogues. All sites are live. What breaks on drift is not uniform, which is what sets severity: two of the five ARE effect-guarded, three are not. If the tracker's threshold moved to three samples, or Record began collapsing identical consecutive samples, then MQTT-disconnected, matter-bridge-listener-lost and recovery-failed would silently report DEGRADED instead of UNHEALTHY while their tests stayed green — and DEGRADED sits below the level health.ServiceAvailability treats as a hard failure. Medium: silent under-reporting on the diagnostic surface for three subsystems, with the guard that would catch it present for only two.
stands.divergence: None found — the five copies and the tracker agree today. I looked specifically for one: Record (tracker.go:214-243) appends every sample without de-duplication, and the event bus serialises dispatch behind a single b.dispatch mutex (internal/central/events/bus.go:245, 260-273), so no concurrent healthy sample can land between the paired Record calls on the same component. The MQTT and Matter probes record on their own component names, so they cannot interleave with the adapter's either. Reporting no diverging input rather than constructing a plausible one.
stands.deadCopy: None. health_wiring.go is reached via WireHealth (exercised in production wiring); mqtt/health_probe.go probeOnce and matter/bridge/health_probe.go are both non-test production functions; tracker.go:214 Record is the single write path all of them use.
stands.guard: Partial — this is the load-bearing detail. Two sites are guarded by the effect: internal/central/adapter/health_wiring_test.go:51-52 (`if got.Status != health.StatusUnhealthy { t.Fatalf("failed → unhealthy (escalated), got %s", got.Status) }`) and :68-69 (breaker open → StatusUnhealthy) run against the real health.Tracker, so they would bite if the threshold moved. Three sites are not. (a) The RecoveryFailedEvent pair at health_wiring.go:159-160 has no assertion at all: internal/central/adapter/adapter_multi_unit_test.go:2582-2595 TestWireHealth_RecoveryFailed publishes the event, calls drainBus() and asserts nothing. (b) internal/north/mqtt/health_probe_test.go:92-108 asserts the MECHANISM against a fakeTracker, not the effect — `if len(got) != 2 { t.Fatalf("samples=%d, want 2", len(got)) }` — so it stays green for any tracker threshold whatsoever. stands.secondReason:
