stands.title: The one-second floor for a resumed countdown is duplicated across two restore paths
stands.evidence: Both quotes verified verbatim. restore.go:332-334: "\tif remaining <= 0 {\n\t\tremaining = time.Second\n\t}" immediately before `e.scheduleStateTimer(a, timerKindExit, remaining)` (restore.go:335) in restoreArming (declared restore.go:268). restore.go:568-570: the identical three lines before `e.scheduleAutoRearm(a, a.autoRearmMode, remaining)` (restore.go:571) in restoreAutoRearm (declared restore.go:543). Both live: restoreAutoRearm is called at restore.go:231 and restoreArming at restore.go:240, both from the persisted-state switch in the restore entry point; no _test.go caller. A repo-package grep for `remaining = time.Second` returns exactly these two lines; the third `if remaining <= 0` hit, engine.go:1569, is the countdown tick chain and `return`s rather than flooring, so it is not a third copy. Guard: none — the only tests touching a resumed countdown are restore_test.go:583 TestRestore_StopPersistsFreshRemainingDurations (asserts remaining_ms == 5000, a positive value) and autorearm_test.go:198 TestAutoRearm_RestoreResumesTheRemainingQuietPeriod (20 s of 30 s remain). Neither drives remaining <= 0, so neither would notice if one floor changed or vanished.
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false I would have seen different values at the two sites (e.g. one `time.Second`, one `500 * time.Millisecond`), or only a single occurrence with the other site delegating to a shared helper. The grep of `remaining = time.Second` returned exactly two lines with identical text.
stands.reason: Two byte-identical sentinel blocks governing when an already-expired exit delay (restoreArming) and an already-expired auto-rearm quiet period (restoreAutoRearm) fire after boot. They agree today and nothing pins them together, so a change to one is silent. One qualification to the candidate's damage argument: the other two restore paths deliberately do *not* floor — restorePending escalates straight to trigger on an elapsed deadline (restore.go:365-373) and restoreTriggered finishes the incident (restore.go:466-477) — so the floor is a two-path policy, not a package-wide one a third path would automatically need.
stands.divergence: None. Both sites read `remaining = time.Second` today; I found no input on which they disagree.
stands.deadCopy: Neither — restoreArming and restoreAutoRearm are both dispatched from the restore switch (restore.go:231 and restore.go:240).
stands.guard: None. restore_test.go:583 and autorearm_test.go:198 exercise resumption with a positive remaining duration only; neither reaches the remaining <= 0 branch at either site.

stands.title: The vanished-interface path re-derives the typed interface enum by a bare cast instead of the ResolvedInterface rule used two lines of code away
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false, one of two things would have shown: (a) reconciler.go:294 would derive the enum, e.g. `hmtypes.ParseWireInterfaceID(id).Bare(r.CentralName)`, mirroring line 223 — it does not, the bare cast is the literal text; or (b) grep for stampWireInterfaceIDs would have found no non-test caller, meaning InterfaceID stays bare in production and the cast is correct. hub_wiring.go:205 is a production caller, so branch (b) is closed. Conversely, had the damage claim been true, grep for `hub.InterfaceReachability` outside internal/model/hub would have returned at least one non-test consumer reading `.Interface` or calling `.ResolvedInterface()`; it returns none.
stands.reason: The code-level claim is exactly as stated: reconcileVanishedInterfaces casts the raw id where the sibling path two lines up uses the probe's explicit enum, and in production that id is `<central>-<interface>`, so hmenum.Interface("ccu1-BidCos-RF") is not a valid interface token. Reconciler.CentralName is on the receiver (used at line 297, 302), so Bare(centralName) was available. The stated damage is not: the aggregate does not store the enum and no production code reads the field it is passed to — only tests do. So the wrong enum is computed and immediately discarded. That makes this an inconsistency waiting for a consumer, not a live defect, hence severity low rather than the claimed high. Note the same bare cast on a wire-form id also sits at internal/model/hub/connectivity.go:94 (`Interface: hmenum.Interface(id)` inside List()) and connectivity.go:107 (OnState), which is why emitNotReadyConnectivity at reconciler.go:406 — cited in the candidate as the correct side — is in fact equally wrong: its `entry` comes from conn.List(), so ResolvedInterface() returns the already-miscast wire form rather than falling through.
stands.divergence: Concrete input: central `ccu1`, CCU serves `BidCos-RF`, then stops listing it. Site B (reconciler.go:223, live path) stamps Interface = hmenum.Interface("BidCos-RF") — the enum. Site A (reconciler.go:294, vanished path) stamps Interface = hmenum.Interface("ccu1-BidCos-RF") — not a member of the hmenum.Interface set. Same interface, same aggregate, two different enum values depending on how it went down. Only tests can observe the difference today.
stands.deadCopy: Neither ResolvedInterface method is dead (coordinators' is called at reconciler.go:223, hub's at reconciler.go:406), but the *channel* that carries the enum is test-only: hub.Connectivity.OnUpdate has no production registration — all six registrations are in _test.go files.
stands.guard: TestReconcilerConnectivityFollowsTheProbeMembership (internal/central/coordinators/reconciler_test.go:319) exercises reconcileVanishedInterfaces but builds probes with bare ids (`coordinators.InterfaceReachability{InterfaceID: id, Reachable: true}`, reconciler_test.go:326) and asserts on ConnectivityChangedEvent, which carries no Interface field — so it could not bite on this even with wire-form ids. No other guard found.

stands.title: InterfaceReachability and its ResolvedInterface rule are defined twice, in the coordinator and in the hub model
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false, one of the two would be an alias of the other (`type InterfaceReachability = hub.InterfaceReachability`) or would lack the method — a grep for `func (r InterfaceReachability) ResolvedInterface` would then have returned a single hit. It returns two, in two packages, with textually identical bodies. Had one copy been dead, the `ResolvedInterface()` caller grep would have shown call sites for only one receiver type; it shows one production call site for each.
stands.reason: The duplication is real and both copies are live. The shared fallback rule `if Interface == "" { return hmenum.Interface(InterfaceID) }` is the same rule c001 shows to be wrong once InterfaceID carries the wire form, so a fix to one file genuinely leaves the other stamping a wire id as an enum — and the hub copy is the one reached at reconciler.go:406, via conn.List() (internal/model/hub/connectivity.go:94 `Interface: hmenum.Interface(id)`), so the hub copy is already miscasting today. Severity stays low for the same reason as c001: no production code reads the Interface field on either type, so drift between the two definitions cannot break a live surface. The LatencyMs asymmetry is not a defect — hub_wiring.go:494-501 documents removing that metric feed deliberately. This is a maintainability finding (one identity rule, two homes, no guard) rather than a correctness one.
stands.divergence: No input makes the two ResolvedInterface implementations return different values — the bodies are byte-identical. The divergence is structural: the hub copy has no LatencyMs field, so a hub.InterfaceReachability can never carry the probe latency the coordinator copy holds. The one place they meet, reconciler.go:406, silently uses the hub copy's already-miscast Interface (set by List() at connectivity.go:94) instead of re-deriving it.
stands.deadCopy: Neither. coordinators.InterfaceReachability.ResolvedInterface is called at internal/central/coordinators/reconciler.go:223; hub.InterfaceReachability.ResolvedInterface at internal/central/coordinators/reconciler.go:406. Both are production paths.
stands.guard: None. No test in the repo compares the two definitions or their method bodies; `grep -rn "ResolvedInterface" --include=*_test.go` finds no cross-package comparison.

stands.title: The MASTER OPERATIONS=0 firmware quirk is normalised per-parameter in the adapter but only whole-descriptor in the coordinator, and the coordinator's comment states the adapter's rule as if the two matched
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false, device_pipeline.go:1980 would gate the normalisation on the whole paramset — e.g. `if key == hmenum.ParamsetKeyMaster && allOperationsNone(paramset)` — or device.go:1463 would have no `quirkedDescriptor` gate and admit every zero-operations parameter. I read both loops end to end: the pipeline test is strictly per-parameter (`pd := paramset[name]`, `pd.Operations == hmenum.OperationsNone`), the coordinator test is strictly whole-descriptor. Had the check been dead, the ScheduleParamsetConsistencyCheck grep would have returned only _test.go hits; it returns internal/central/adapter/ccu_wiring.go:1191.
stands.reason: The two rules genuinely disagree on the mixed case, and the coordinator comment misstates the hydration rule: it says hydration normalises "exactly that case" (every MASTER parameter zero), while device_pipeline.go:1980 normalises any single zero unconditionally. So the coordinator's stated justification for dropping lone zeros — "a parameter the CCU does not serve" — is contradicted by the daemon's own behaviour, which serves it as a READ|WRITE data point. Severity is low rather than the claimed medium because the only consumer of the check's result is a log line: internal/central/adapter/ccu_wiring.go:1193-1201 passes an onResult closure whose entire body is `logger.Warn("wire.paramset_inconsistency", ...)`. Drift here costs a missed diagnostic warning about stale HmIPServer descriptors, not a wrong value on any north-bound surface.
stands.divergence: Concrete input: an HmIP MASTER descriptor for channel `000A1BE9957782:1` holding two parameters, `GLOBAL_BUTTON_LOCK` with Operations=3 and `TEMPERATURE_OFFSET` with Operations=0 (the partially-stale descriptor a firmware update leaves behind). Hydration (device_pipeline.go:1980) rewrites TEMPERATURE_OFFSET to READ|WRITE and builds a data point for it (device_pipeline.go:2035 `dpKey, err := hmtypes.NewDataPointKey(...)`, reached because there is no visibility gate). The consistency check (device.go:1463) computes allOperationsNone=false, so expectedParams = {GLOBAL_BUTTON_LOCK} only; TEMPERATURE_OFFSET is never compared against the live GetParamset answer. The channel is reported clean while the daemon publishes a data point the CCU no longer serves.
stands.deadCopy: Neither. The pipeline normalisation runs on every MASTER hydration; the coordinator check runs from internal/central/adapter/ccu_wiring.go:1191 after each HmIP-RF ingest.
stands.guard: TestCheckParamsetConsistencyDetectsStaleParamsReportedWithoutOperations (internal/central/coordinators/device_coordinator_cache_restore_test.go:495) — verified: its fixture is a single-parameter paramset `{"PARAM_QUIRKED": {Operations: hmenum.OperationsNone}}` (line 510-512), i.e. the all-zero case where the two rules agree. Its own doc comment asserts the pipeline rule the way the coordinator comment does: `// pins the firmware quirk the check exists for: an HmIPServer that reports\n// OPERATIONS=0 for MASTER parameters.` No test covers a mixed descriptor. No guard would fail if the two rules drifted further apart.

stands.title: "Which part of an address is the device" is decided four times in this package, with two different colon conventions
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false, link.go:263 would delegate the way event.go:538 does (`return hmtypes.DeviceAddress(s)`) and a repo-wide grep for a backwards colon scan would return a single implementation. It returns three (link.go:263, adapter/devices.go:237, hmproto/device.go:152) against two first-colon implementations (hmtypes/address.go:71, event.go:300) and one inline prefix match (cache.go:551). Had one copy been dead, the caller grep would have shown only _test.go hits for it; every copy has non-test callers.
stands.reason: The duplication and the two conventions are exactly as described, and the candidate's own scoping of the damage is correct: for a well-formed Homematic address with exactly one colon (`VCU1234567:3`) all implementations agree, so nothing is observably wrong today. I searched for a producer of a two-colon address and did not find one either — the one string in this area that carries two colons, internal/central/coordinators/device.go:1484 `missingForDevice = append(missingForDevice, chAddr+\":\"+param)`, is a diagnostic label that never reaches a splitter. I am not asserting that no such producer exists; I am reporting that I did not locate one, which is why this stays a duplication finding at low severity rather than a correctness one. The cost is that the address grammar cannot be changed in one place, and it is now six implementations rather than the four claimed — the candidate undercounted.
stands.divergence: No diverging input found among real production producers. The conventions diverge only on an address with two or more colons: for `ABC123:1:2`, hmtypes.DeviceAddress / event.go:300 return `ABC123`, while link.go:263, adapter/devices.go:237 and hmproto.DeviceDescription.ChannelNo cut at the last colon and return `ABC123:1` (ChannelNo → 2, not 1). cache.go:551 is a third rule again: a prefix match, so evicting device `ABC123:1` would match the entry `ABC123:1:2` that the first-colon rule assigns to device `ABC123`. I could not identify any component that emits such an address, so this divergence is latent, not observed.
stands.deadCopy: None. link.go:263 ← link.go:254; cache.go:551 ← cache.go:469 (DeviceRemovedEvent); event.go:538 ← event.go:238; adapter/devices.go:237 ← ~30 call sites in internal/central/adapter; hmtypes/address.go:71 and hmproto/device.go:152 are both widely called.
stands.guard: None. No test asserts that the address-splitting implementations agree, and no test feeds a two-colon address through more than one of them.

stands.title: The CCU `error` callback code decoder is written out twice, near-verbatim, in the two listeners
stands.evidence: Both quotes verified verbatim. internal/central/rpcserver/xmlrpc_server.go:451-461: '\t\t// error_code arrives as either an integer or a stringified / \t\t// integer depending on the CCU firmware. Try int first; fall / \t\t// back to string-parse. / \t\tvar code int / \t\tif i, err := xmlrpc.AsInt(params[1]); err == nil { / \t\t\tcode = i / \t\t} else if s, err := xmlrpc.AsString(params[1]); err == nil { / \t\t\t_, _ = fmt.Sscanf(s, "%d", &code) / \t\t} / \t\tmsg, _ := xmlrpc.AsString(params[2]) / \t\t_ = h.Error(ctx, iface, code, msg)'. internal/central/rpcserver/binrpc_server.go:543-551: '\t\tvar code int / \t\tif i, err := xmlrpc.AsInt(rest[0]); err == nil { / \t\t\tcode = i / \t\t} else if s, err := xmlrpc.AsString(rest[0]); err == nil { / \t\t\t_, _ = fmt.Sscanf(s, "%d", &code) / \t\t} / \t\tmsg, _ := xmlrpc.AsString(rest[1]) / \t\t_ = handlers.Error(ctx, ifaceID, code, msg)'. Both listeners are constructed from the composition root: cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_helpers.go:134 'srv, err := rpcserver.NewXMLRPCServer(xcfg)' and cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_boot.go:446 'srv, binErr := rpcserver.NewBINRPCServer(binCfg)'. Both feed the same handler contract, internal/central/rpcserver/handlers.go:50 'Error(ctx context.Context, interfaceID string, errorCode int, msg string) error'.
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false, only one of the two server files would contain the decode. 'grep -rln Sscanf internal/central/rpcserver/' returns both internal/central/rpcserver/xmlrpc_server.go and internal/central/rpcserver/binrpc_server.go.
stands.reason: Two live copies of one decoding rule behind one shared handler interface, with nothing pinning them together. Damage on drift is bounded — a CCU fault classified differently per transport, and both copies silently map an undecodable code to 0 — so this stays low, not because the duplication is unreal.
stands.divergence: None found. The two bodies are token-identical apart from the argument index (params[1]/params[2] vs rest[0]/rest[1]), and both arity checks are equivalent (xmlrpc_server.go:448 'len(params) != 3' vs binrpc_server.go:541 'len(rest) != 2'). No input distinguishes them today.
stands.deadCopy: none — both listeners are constructed at the composition root
stands.guard: none. internal/central/rpcserver/xmlrpc_dispatch_test.go:912-930 (TestBINRPCDispatchErrorWithStringCode) drives only the BIN-RPC side and asserts only 'h.errorCalls.Load() == 1' — it never checks the decoded value, so it would stay green if the string branch produced 0 instead of -7, and it touches the XML-RPC copy not at all.

stands.title: Three comments in internal/central describe a CCU-facing interface_id format the producer no longer emits
stands.evidence: Quotes verified verbatim. internal/central/bootstrap.go:43-45: '\t// Daemon-global instance identity — the leading component of every / \t// central'\''s wire interface_id (`<instance_name>-<ccu_name>-<iface>`, / \t// ADR-0024). Same for every central in this daemon.' internal/central/central.go:45-52: '\t// InstanceName is the daemon'\''s own identity, advertised to the CCU / \t// as the leading component of the wire interface_id / \t// (`<instance_name>-<central_name>-<interface>`) so two daemons against / \t// the same CCU do not overwrite each other'\''s callback registration. / \t// Daemon-global (same for every central); defaults to the OS / \t// hostname. Empty falls back to the legacy `<central_name>-<interface>` / \t// form. See ADR-0024. / \tInstanceName string'. A third, unlisted copy of the same stale claim: internal/central/central.go:456-461 '// InstanceName returns the daemon-global instance identity used as the / // leading component of the wire interface_id. Empty when unset (the / // interface_id then falls back to the legacy `<central_name>-<interface>` / // form).' The actual producer, internal/central/adapter/interface_id.go:29-31 and :54-64: '// InitInterfaceID returns the wire-boundary interface identifier the daemon / // advertises to the CCU at init()/deinit() … Format: / // `loom-<instance_name>-<central_name>-<interface>`.' / 'func InitInterfaceID(instanceName, centralName string, iface hmenum.Interface) string { / \tparts := make([]string, 0, 4) / \tparts = append(parts, IDPrefix) / \tif instanceName != "" && instanceName != centralName { parts = append(parts, instanceName) } / \tif centralName != "" { parts = append(parts, centralName) } / \treturn strings.Join(append(parts, string(iface)), "-") }' with 'const IDPrefix = "loom"' (interface_id.go:27). InitInterfaceID is the live producer: internal/central/adapter/ccu_wiring.go:735 'initID := InitInterfaceID(unit.InstanceName(), cc.Name, iface)' and internal/central/adapter/cuxd_wiring.go:63 (same line); the value bootstrap.go:46 injects ('instanceName := cfg.North.Discovery.MDNS.ResolveInstanceName()', passed as Config.InstanceName at :53) reaches it through Unit.InstanceName() (central.go:461). The pre-prefix form survives only as an explicit legacy variant, adapter/interface_id.go:79 LegacyInitInterfaceID, used solely for BIN-RPC de-registration (cuxd_wiring.go:188, :297). The third, contradicting sentence the candidate cites is real: internal/central/interface_id.go:22-24 '// … The daemon hostname (instance name) is deliberately NOT / // part of this id: it would leak into MQTT topics and the external API / // and make the surface host-dependent.' — that one is about the internal WireInterfaceID (`<central_name>-<interface>`), a different identifier.
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false, InitInterfaceID would have joined instanceName/centralName/iface without a leading token. If they had matched, I would have found either two increments outside their retriers or two inside.

stands.title: "The CCU speaks Latin-1" is implemented four different ways across the transports, and the fourth copy is dead
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false I would have seen one of two things, and saw neither: (a) a single shared helper called from all four sites — instead each site calls golang.org/x/text/encoding/charmap directly or hand-rolls its own byte loop (jsonrpc/client.go:832 latin1ToUTF8, duplicated again as internal/central/adapter/hub_wiring.go:1656 latin1ToUTF8String, byte-for-byte the same algorithm on a different type); or (b) the same gating condition at each site — instead `grep -n "utf8.Valid"` finds the gate only in jsonrpc/client.go:335, hub_wiring.go:1631 and text_utils.go:39, while xmlrpc/message.go:46,:73, binrpc/encode.go:154 and binrpc/decode.go:250 transcode unconditionally. For the dead-copy leg the control is the grep itself: a live FixXMLRPCEncoding would have produced at least one non-_test.go hit; it produced zero.
stands.divergence: The two response bytes 0xC3 0xBC (a CCU object name storing UTF-8 "ü" — the case pkg/hmtypes/text_utils.go:12-19 says the CCU actually does: "stores user-defined strings (link names, room names, …) as raw UTF-8 bytes inside an ISO-8859-1 XML document"). Over JSON-RPC, utf8.Valid(raw) is true at client.go:335, the branch is skipped, and the string decodes as "ü". Over BIN-RPC the same two bytes hit decode.go:250 unconditionally and become U+00C3 U+00BC — "Ã¼". Over XML-RPC the document's own ISO-8859-1 declaration drives charset.NewReaderLabel (message.go:189) to the same "Ã¼", and the helper written to repair precisely that (FixXMLRPCEncoding) is never called. Same logical datum, three different rendered values.
stands.deadCopy: pkg/hmtypes/text_utils.go:27 FixXMLRPCEncoding — 7 tests in pkg/hmtypes/text_utils_test.go, zero production callers. It is the only copy that repairs UTF-8-inside-ISO-8859-1 on the XML-RPC leg, so the repair passes its tests while the live XML-RPC path never performs it.
stands.guard: None cross-transport. `grep -rn "ISO-8859|ISO8859|latin1|Latin1|Latin-1" tests/` returns zero hits, so no contract or e2e test compares the transports' policies. Per-transport tests only pin each policy in isolation: internal/client/transport/jsonrpc/client_charset_test.go (TestClientDecodesLatin1Body, TestClientKeepsValidUTF8Body, TestLatin1ToUTF8), internal/client/transport/xmlrpc/message_test.go, internal/client/transport/binrpc/codec_test.go. Nothing would fail if one policy changed.
stands.reason: The candidate's quotes are exact and its structural claim understates the spread: the knowledge is implemented four times, not three, and the fourth implementation is dead. The three transport policies are not simply redundant — a byte-oriented ISO-8859-1 wire (BIN-RPC, and XML-RPC's declared preamble) genuinely requires unconditional transcoding, while JSON-RPC's spec mandates UTF-8 and only needs a heuristic for CCU violations, so this is not a plain 'two readings of one datum' pair. What makes it a real finding rather than a style complaint is the measured divergence above plus the unwired repair: the JSON-RPC and ReGa legs both handle the UTF-8-inside-Latin-1 case, the XML-RPC leg has a tested helper for it that no production code calls, and no guard anywhere would notice if the policies drifted further. Severity low: the exposure is rendered-name/unit mojibake on the XML-RPC and BIN-RPC read paths, not control-path corruption, and daemon-owned device naming flows through the separately-correct decodeRegaField path (internal/central/adapter/hub_wiring.go:1619). One input I did not measure and will not infer: whether current CCU firmware actually emits UTF-8 bytes inside its ISO-8859-1 XML-RPC documents. text_utils.go:12-19 asserts it does, but that is a code comment, not a wire capture — establishing it needs a live XML-RPC read of a paramset carrying a non-ASCII unit or a link name. The code-level divergence stands regardless of the answer; the user-visible blast radius does not.

stands.title: The 13-month hourly-tier retention default is defined once in config and once in the recorder, and the recorder's copy is unreachable in production
stands.evidence:
Both quotes verified verbatim.

internal/config/config.go:461-465:
  "// RetentionHourlyDefault is how long the hourly rollup tier is kept when\n// the operator did not override it: 13 months, chosen so a full year of\n// hourly resolution survives even a slightly late rollout of the daily\n// tier's consumers (e.g. the energy view's month-over-month comparisons).\nconst RetentionHourlyDefault = 13 * 30 * 24 * time.Hour"

internal/history/recorder.go:36-39:
  "\t// DefaultRetentionHourly is how long the hourly rollup tier is kept\n\t// by default (13 months) — long enough that a year of hourly\n\t// resolution survives even a slightly late read of the tier.\n\tDefaultRetentionHourly = 13 * 30 * 24 * time.Hour"

Both are live symbols in production packages, but only one is reachable at runtime.

Production consumers, by grep over *.go (whole repo):
- `history.New(` appears at exactly two production sites: cmd/openccu-loom/history_wiring.go:83 and :135. Nothing else in the repo constructs a Recorder (no _test.go site either, except internal/history/recorder_test.go:619 which calls the package-local New).
- Both literals set the field: history_wiring.go:85 and :142 both read "RetentionHourly: hc.RetentionHourlyOrDefault(),".
- internal/config/config.go:477-482: "func (c HistoryConfig) RetentionHourlyOrDefault() time.Duration {\n\tif c.RetentionHourly > 0 {\n\t\treturn c.RetentionHourly\n\t}\n\treturn RetentionHourlyDefault\n}" — both branches return a value > 0 (the constant is 9360h).
- Therefore internal/history/recorder.go:153-155, "\tif r.retentionHourly <= 0 {\n\t\tr.retentionHourly = DefaultRetentionHourly\n\t}", cannot fire from either production caller. DefaultRetentionHourly's only non-comment reference in the whole repo is that one line (grep for the identifier returns recorder.go:36, :39, :109, :154 and nothing else).
- No clamp elsewhere can push RetentionHourly to <= 0: internal/config/config.go:2092-2093 clamps only the raw tier ("if h := &c.Persistence.History; h.Retention > 0 && h.Retention < HistoryRetentionFloor { h.Retention = HistoryRetentionFloor"). RetentionHourly is never rewritten at load.

Guard: none. No _test.go in the repo imports internal/history except cmd/openccu-loom/central_adopt_test.go:22, and no test anywhere mentions DefaultRetentionHourly or asserts the two constants are equal. internal/history/recorder_test.go:619 pins RetentionHourly explicitly ("r := New(store, Options{RetentionHourly: time.Hour})"), so even the fallback branch is untested.
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false I would have seen at least one of: (a) a third production `history.New(`/`history.Options{` site — grep returned exactly two, both in cmd/openccu-loom/history_wiring.go, both setting RetentionHourly; (b) a path where RetentionHourlyOrDefault can return <= 0 (a `>=`/`!=` bug or a negative clamp) making recorder.go:154 reachable — config.go:477-482 returns c.RetentionHourly only when > 0, else a positive constant, and nothing rewrites the field at load; (c) a guard test comparing config.RetentionHourlyDefault against history.DefaultRetentionHourly — the identifier grep found no test reference at all. Any one of those greps hitting would have produced `refuted` (for a/b) or a named guard (for c).
stands.reason: The duplication is real and both quotes are verbatim. The two constants are not two readings of one datum — they answer the same question ("how long is the hourly rollup tier kept when the operator sets nothing") with the same expression in two packages, and only one of them is consulted at runtime. Severity is low rather than medium because nothing in the running daemon breaks when they drift: every production Recorder receives the config-resolved value, so changing internal/config/config.go:465 alone changes daemon behaviour correctly and completely. What drifts is documentation and test ground truth — internal/history/recorder.go:37-38 and :109 would still advertise 13 months, and any future Options literal that omits RetentionHourly (plausible for an exporter- or retention-only path) would silently inherit the stale value with no guard to catch it. That latent risk is what keeps it a finding rather than noise.
stands.divergence: None today: both expressions are literally `13 * 30 * 24 * time.Hour` = 9360h, so no input exists on which the two copies already disagree. The drift is prospective, not present.
stands.deadCopy: internal/history/recorder.go:39 (DefaultRetentionHourly). Its single non-comment reference is internal/history/recorder.go:154, inside a `retentionHourly <= 0` branch that neither production constructor (cmd/openccu-loom/history_wiring.go:85, :142) can reach, and no test exercises it either.

stands.title: The row-write paramset is built three times inside textdisplay
stands.evidence: Quote verified at all three cited lines. :556 (inside Write) and :692 (inside WriteWithSound) both open `		values := map[string]any{` followed verbatim by `			string(hmenum.ParameterDisplayDataID):     r.ID,` / `			string(hmenum.ParameterDisplayDataCommit): true,` / the comment `// STRING is always sent, even when empty — an empty string clears the` `// display row. Skipping it leaves the previous text visible.` / `			string(hmenum.ParameterDisplayDataString): r.Text,`. I diffed :556-583 against :692-719 after normalising the only differing token (`iconValue` vs `iconValueWS`): the two blocks are byte-identical — icon-head fallback (`if len(t.availableIcons) > 0 { … = t.availableIcons[0] } else { … = noIcon }`) and the three guarded formatting fields (ALIGNMENT / TEXT_COLOR / BG_COLOR, each behind `!= nil && *… != ""`). The third copy is `writeRowFields` at :777, which re-emits the same field set as sequential SetValue calls, minus COMMIT (deliberate — Write/WriteWithSound call `t.Commit` after it) and with the icon fallback spelled a third time at :787-793 as `iconValueFB`. The drift precedent the candidate cites is real and at the cited place: textdisplay.go:619-622 `// atomically. A second implementation drifted from all four — it skipped the` `// defaults, so a row arrived without the colours the device expects, and it` `// deferred a single trailing commit, so a failure midway left some rows` `// applied and others staged.` Liveness: Write and WriteWithSound both have production callers — internal/central/adapter/custom_dp_dispatcher.go:727 `return t.WriteWithSound(ctx, row, opts, prio)` and :730 `return t.Write(ctx, row, prio)`, plus internal/model/custom/textdisplay/payload.go:193 `return t.WriteWithSound(ctx, r, opts, priority)`. Guard: the cited TestTextDisplayWriteWithSoundIncludesSoundParams (textdisplay_deep_test.go:146) drives the *fallback* writer (`w := &stubWriter{}`), so it pins copy C, not A or B. The paramset copies are covered by TestTextDisplayWriteAtomicPutParamset (textdisplay_test.go:60) and TestTextDisplayWriteWithSoundAtomicPutParamset (:99) — but the second asserts only SOUND / REPETITIONS / INTERVAL (:113-124) and never checks ID, STRING, ICON, ALIGNMENT or the colours. No test compares copy A against copy B. So dropping ICON or the empty-STRING rule from the WriteWithSound copy alone leaves the whole suite green.
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false I would have seen one of two things, and saw neither. (1) The diff of :556-583 against :692-719 would have printed hunks, or one entry point would have delegated to a shared builder rather than reopening `values := map[string]any{` — the normalised diff printed nothing and exited 0. (2) `grep -rn --include='*.go' -E "WriteWithSound|WriteRows|textdisplay.TextDisplay" . | grep -v _test.go` would have returned only comment lines for one of the two entry points — instead it returned executable calls in internal/central/adapter/custom_dp_dispatcher.go and internal/model/custom/textdisplay/payload.go for both. For the dead-copy half: had copy C been live, some production ChannelWriter would have lacked PutParamset; internal/model/device/channel_set.go:104 makes PutParamset mandatory on the interface, and the concrete wrapper `operationLockedWriter` implements both SetValue (channel_write_guard.go:36) and PutParamset (:52) with signatures identical to generic.ParamsetWriter (datapoint.go:47-56), so the type assertion at :555 and :691 always succeeds.
stands.reason: Three literal constructions of one wire bundle, all three verified verbatim at the cited lines, with two of the three entry points reachable from the live dispatcher and no test tying them together. Severity low rather than medium because the blast radius on drift is one device profile (HmIP-WRCD, the only text-display model per the WriteRows comment at :608-611) and the failure mode is a display row rendered with stale text/icon or missing colours while the sound plays — operator-visible, but no data loss, no safety or auth impact, and no cross-central effect. What raises it above cosmetic is the guard shape: TestTextDisplayWriteWithSoundAtomicPutParamset checks only the three sound keys, so a formatting field added to Write but forgotten in WriteWithSound ships green.
stands.divergence: None found today. The two paramset copies are byte-identical modulo the local variable name (`iconValue` at :566-574 vs `iconValueWS` at :702-710); a normalised diff of :556-583 against :692-719 is empty. Copy C differs only by omitting DISPLAY_DATA_COMMIT, which is correct for its caller (Write:588 and WriteWithSound:751 call t.Commit separately). I have no concrete diverging input to name — the finding rests on the absence of a linking guard, not on an existing disagreement.
stands.deadCopy: internal/model/custom/textdisplay/textdisplay.go:777 (writeRowFields) is unreachable in production. It is entered only from the `else` side of `if pw, ok := t.Writer.(generic.ParamsetWriter); ok` at :555 and :691. The production writer arrives via init.go:48 `td := New(ch.Address, ch.Writer())`; Channel.Writer() (channel_set.go:252-260) returns `&operationLockedWriter{origin: c, next: w}`, which implements SetValue (channel_write_guard.go:36) and PutParamset (:52) with the exact signatures of generic.ParamsetWriter, and internal/model/device/channel_set.go:104 makes PutParamset mandatory on every ChannelWriter — the concrete one installed at internal/central/adapter/device_pipeline.go:1862/1898 is `&channelWriterAdapter{…}`, whose PutParamset is at internal/central/adapter/bound_writer.go:117. stands.title: 0..1 to 0..100 half-up rounding is implemented twice
stands.evidence: Quote verified verbatim. blind.go:351: `		s := fmt.Sprintf("L2=%d,L=%d", int(wireT*100+0.5), int(wireL*100+0.5))`. mixins.go:430-431: `// OpenFraction returns the position as a 0–100 percentage.` / `func (p Position) OpenFraction() int { return int(p.level*100 + 0.5) }`. BOTH SIDES LIVE: blind.go:351 sits in Blind.sendCombined (blind.go:316), whose production callers are blind.go:249, :269 and :412 (SetPosition / SetTilt / SetCombined paths) — non-test callers confirmed by grep -rn sendCombined --include='*.go' internal/ filtered against _test.go. OpenFraction has five production callers, all in internal/model/custom/cover/payload.go — :84, :215, :222, :321. Neither is test-only. Both operate on the SAME domain: sendCombined clamps its inputs to [0,1] at blind.go:317-324 (`if level < 0 { level = 0 }` … `if tilt > 1 { tilt = 1 }`) and NewPosition clamps identically at mixins.go:418-424, so the two expressions are the same rule over the same input range, written out twice.
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false, one of two things would have shown: (a) blind.go:351 would have called a shared helper — the way its sibling branch does, blind.go:349 `parameter.ConvertHMLevelToCPV(wireL)`, which centralises the HM-side conversion in internal/parameter/converter.go:269-277 — or (b) the two expressions would have operated on different input domains, making them two readings of one datum rather than one rule twice. Neither holds: the IP branch inlines the arithmetic while the HM branch delegates, and both call sites clamp to [0,1] first.
stands.divergence: None today — both expressions are literally the same arithmetic, so no input separates them. The reachable drift is concrete and worth naming, because the existing tests cannot see it: levels 0.29, 0.57 and 0.58 are the class where half-up and truncation part company (0.29*100 = 28.999999999999996 in binary64 → half-up 29, truncate 28; 0.57 → 56.99999999999999 → 57 vs 56; 0.58 → 57.99999999999999 → 58 vs 57), and payload.go:79-83 records exactly this class as an already-fixed display bug. Every value pinned by the write-side tests — 0.5, 0.75, 0.4, 0.9, 0.3 (blind_test.go:257/278, blind_target_staleness_test.go:144/177/211/260/272) — and by the read-side test, 0.81 (parity_test.go:66), multiplies to an exact or above-integer float, so all of them yield the same digit under truncation as under half-up. A truncation regression in either copy would therefore leave both suites green.
stands.deadCopy: Neither. Production callers listed above for both.
stands.guard: None that couples the copies. Each side has its own pinned expectations — blind_test.go:257 `want := "L2=75,L=50"`, blind_target_staleness_test.go:144 `"L2=0,L=50"`, parity_test.go:66-67 `p.OpenFraction() != 81` — but they share no source of truth, and (per the divergence field) none of their pinned levels falls in the class that distinguishes rounding modes, so they would not even catch a unilateral change of rounding mode.
stands.reason: Confirmed as a genuine duplication, not an EnumLabel/EnumLabelFromWire-shaped pair: same conversion, same clamped [0,1] domain, differing only in which quantity is fed in (commanded target vs observed position). Severity stays low because nothing diverges today and the failure mode is a one-percent disagreement between the position HA displays and the position written to the device — cosmetic-to-annoying, not a correctness or safety break — and because the two quantities meet only after a CCU echo, which normalises them. The finding's weight is that the drift is invisible to the current suites, per the divergence field. Note the asymmetry that makes the duplication avoidable: the HM branch one line up already delegates to a shared helper (parameter.ConvertHMLevelToCPV), so the IP branch is the odd one out.

stands.title: Two different definitions of 'calculated sensor state change', with a comment asserting they are the same
stands.evidence:
All four quotes verified verbatim. data_point.go:135 `func (s *DewPointSensor) IsStateChange() bool { return s.IsRefreshed() && !s.StateUncertain() }`. state_change_with.go:38 `// Without options the method is equivalent to [DewPointSensor.IsStateChange].` and :40-42 `func (s *DewPointSensor) IsStateChangeWith(opts ...StateChangeOpt) bool { return calcIsStateChangeWith(s.IsRefreshedFromSources(), s.StateUncertain(), opts) }`. climate.go:536 `func (s *DewPointSensor) IsRefreshed() bool { return s.emit.refreshed() }`, and climate.go:53-58 `// refreshed reports whether the sensor has emitted at least one computed value.` / `return es.hasLast`. state_uncertain.go:266-279 `func (ss *sourceSink) IsRefreshedFromSources() bool { srcs := ss.snapshotSources(); if len(srcs) == 0 { return false }; for _, dp := range srcs { _, observed := dp.RawValue(); if !observed { return false } }; return true }`.

The predicates are provably different: `hasLast` is set only inside emitState.feed (climate.go:72-91), which returns early on `if !ok`, on `if sink.PublishedEventRecently()` and on `if !shouldPublishCalcUpdate(sources)` — all before `es.last, es.hasLast = value, true`. IsRefreshedFromSources asks only whether every source DP has an observed RawValue, which is true well before any emission happens. The pattern repeats for all eight sensor types (state_change_with.go:40-77 vs data_point.go:135/186/239/294/347/404/463/519).
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false, IsStateChangeWith would have been written as `calcIsStateChangeWith(s.IsRefreshed(), ...)` — the same predicate the no-option method uses — or IsRefreshed and IsRefreshedFromSources would resolve to the same expression. They resolve to `es.hasLast` and a loop over source RawValue observability respectively, in two different files.
stands.reason: The doc comment at state_change_with.go:38 asserts an equivalence the code does not have. But I checked callers before rating it: grepping `\.IsStateChange()` and `IsStateChangeWith(` across internal and pkg (excluding _test.go) finds NO production consumer of either method on any calculated sensor — every hit is the declaration itself or an unrelated typed IsStateChange on custom/combined DPs (siren.go:274, valve.go:121, cover, combined/data_point.go:89/187). So the described damage (a caller switching to the option form and silently changing semantics) is a future hazard, not a live defect. That places this as a false comment on unconsumed API surface: low severity.
stands.divergence: Concrete: a DewPointSensor whose TEMPERATURE and HUMIDITY source DPs have both been observed, but where emitState.feed has not yet set hasLast — e.g. both sources published inside the same 500 ms CCU burst so `shouldPublishCalcUpdate(sources)` returns false (climate.go:81-83), or the formula returned ok=false (climate.go:72-74). stands.title: Group.Usage claims to mirror the operation-mode gate its members apply, and does not
stands.negativeControl: Had a north-bound surface consumed Group.Usage, the eight-site grep would have shown a call on a value obtained from Channel.EventGroups() or EventGroupForKind (internal/model/device/channel.go:1238,1257). It showed the type-asserted call at eventbridge.go:1899 on a generic dp instead, so the grep did surface the interface-shaped call pattern and simply found no group behind it.
stands.divergence: A channel whose CHANNEL_OPERATION_MODE excludes every keypress parameter: each Source.Usage() returns hmenum.DataPointUsageIgnored (event.go:338), while the Group.Usage() over exactly those sources returns hmenum.DataPointUsageEvent (group.go:114). The comment's 'at least one member is explicitly enabled' condition is never evaluated - g.sources is not read.
stands.deadCopy: Group.Usage() itself. No production caller, so the visible-event-entity outcome the candidate describes cannot occur on any current surface.
stands.guard: None. No test asserts a relationship between Group.Usage and its members' Usage.
stands.reason: Confirmed as stated in the title: the doc comment describes a membership-dependent rule that the body does not implement, and the sibling Source.Usage does implement the gate the comment invokes. I downgrade to low and correct the damage: 'a group ... still advertises itself as a visible event entity' is unverified - Group.Usage has no consumer, so today the method misleads a reader (the CLAUDE.md comment-claim failure mode) rather than mis-rendering an entity. 'The doc comment states the opposite of what the body does' is slightly overstated: the comment is silent on the all-members-disabled case; what it asserts falsely is that the body inspects members at all.

stands.title: The HA discovery topic prefix is a model format string and an adapter string literal
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false, the sweep would have obtained its prefix from the model layer (a naming-level constant or helper), and `grep -rn 'homeassistant/' --include='*.go'` filtered to non-test files would have hit only internal/model/naming/. It hit five production sites in internal/north/mqtt/ carrying the literal independently.
stands.reason: The duplication is real and both halves are live. Severity downgraded from medium to low, and the candidate's damage scenario does not hold today: I grepped the whole repo for a configurable discovery prefix (`discovery_prefix`, `DiscoveryPrefix`, `HAPrefix` across *.go and *.yaml) and found nothing — the prefix is a hard-coded literal on both sides, so there is no input on which producer and sweep disagree now. What is left is a latent coupling that only bites if someone makes the prefix configurable. One of the two sweeps is already guarded (see `guard`); the unscoped one is not. Note also that internal/north/mqtt/birth_sync.go:19 is weaker evidence than the candidate implies: `homeassistant/status` is HA's lifecycle topic, not a discovery-config topic — it shares the prefix word but not the topic grammar.
stands.guard: Partial. internal/north/mqtt/retain_cleanup_ownership_test.go:302-312 (TestDiscoveryOrphanSweepRetractsTheOldEventObject) builds the topic through the producer — 'oldTopic := b.Topics().DiscoveryConfig("event", nodeID, "1_event")' — seeds it, runs 'b.RunDiscoveryOrphanCleanupOnce(...)' and fatals on 'if n == 0'. A producer-side prefix change with retain_cleanup.go:757 unchanged makes the sweep's HasPrefix reject the topic, n becomes 0, and the test fails. NO equivalent guard for the unscoped sweep: internal/north/mqtt/unscoped_discovery_cleanup_test.go:44-47 hard-codes its topics as string constants ('unscopedTopic = "homeassistant/event/ccu_bidcos-rf/10_event/config"'), so it never touches the producer and would stay green through a prefix drift at retain_cleanup.go:1116/:1130.
stands.divergence: None found. Both spellings are the identical literal `homeassistant/` today, and no config field exists that could make them differ. The divergence is latent, not present.

stands.title: Two translation-key slug grammars that claim the same source and produce different slugs
stands.negativeControl: Had the two grammars agreed, tracing a name containing a character outside [a-z0-9_.-] through both would have produced the same string. It does not — see divergence — and the divergence is anchored on a value the repo itself asserts as expected output, so the difference cannot be an artefact of my tracing.
stands.reason: The duplication and the divergence are real and I have a concrete separating input taken from the repo's own test data. The candidate's severity of `high` is refuted, and the reason is the strongest fact here: NEITHER copy has a production caller. device.GenerateTranslationKey's only call site in the whole repo is tests/golden/naming_test.go:362 (`tk := device.GenerateTranslationKey(fullName)`), which writes it into the golden snapshot's `translation_key` column — a golden that pins behaviour nothing ships. generic.generateTranslationKey reaches production only via `(*DataPoint[T]).TranslationKey()` at parity_accessors.go:46-47, and `grep -rn "\\.TranslationKey()" --include="*.go" .` excluding tests returns only internal/north/rest/handlers/event_groups.go:85 and internal/model/event/group.go:95, both of which call `event.Group.TranslationKey()` → `event.GenerateTranslationKey(Kind)` (internal/model/event/event.go:382), a third, unrelated grammar (strip the "homematic." prefix, replace dots). So the candidate's damage statement — a consumer keyed on the slug missing on whichever path it did not generate — has no consumer to happen to today. Severity low: latent inconsistency plus a golden test recording an unshipped grammar.
stands.divergence: Input `"Wohnzimmer Licht"` (a case the repo already asserts, internal/model/device/naming_test.go:82 `{"Wohnzimmer Licht", "wohnzimmer_licht"}`): device.GenerateTranslationKey returns `"wohnzimmer_licht"` (space hits the `default:` arm at naming.go:52-57 and becomes an underscore); generic.generateTranslationKey returns `"wohnzimmerlicht"` (space hits `default: // drop all other characters` at parity_accessors.go:33-35). The candidate's own example also holds: `"PM 2.5"` → `"pm_2_5"` (device) vs `"pm2_5"` (generic).
stands.deadCopy: Both. internal/model/device/naming.go:39 has no production caller (only tests/golden/naming_test.go:362 and internal/model/device/naming_test.go:89). internal/model/generic/parity_accessors.go:20 is called only from (*DataPoint[T]).TranslationKey() at :47, which itself has no production call site.
stands.guard: None that crosses the two. internal/model/device/naming_test.go:78-92 and internal/model/generic/datapoint_parity_accessors_test.go:371 each assert their own copy in isolation; both would stay green under any divergence between them.

stands.title: The forced-sensor '_sensor' suffix decision is applied at three independent sites
stands.negativeControl: Had a cross-plane guard existed, `grep -rln "ForcedSensorSuffix" tests/` would have returned a test comparing an MQTT unique_id against the model/REST one; it returns nothing under tests/ at all. Had the goldens covered it implicitly, a suffixed row would appear in the snapshots; `grep -o "LEVEL_sensor" tests/integration/testdata/model_snapshot_openccu-loom.json` and the same grep against discovery_snapshot_openccu-loom.json both return nothing. Had the string itself been duplicable, the grep would have shown a literal "_sensor" beside the constant; it does not.
stands.reason: Confirmed exactly as the candidate framed it, including its own severity. The constant is shared so the string cannot drift, and the decision predicate turns out to be shared too (both sides bottom out in generic.IsForceSensorParameter), so there is no diverging input today. What is genuinely unpinned is the identity itself across planes: only the generic site is tested, and nothing would catch a fourth identifier builder that omits the suffix, or an ordering change that let a plane read the flag before ApplyForceSensorMarks set it.
stands.divergence: None. Both predicates resolve to generic.IsForceSensorParameter(model, parameter) — directly at internal/north/mqtt/discovery.go:502, transitively at internal/store/visibility/operation_mode.go:535 → MarkForcedSensor → IsForcedSensor for the other two — and the appended string is the single constant internal/model/datapoint/base.go:293.
stands.deadCopy: Neither. All three sites have production callers.
stands.guard: None across the three. internal/model/generic/payload_test.go:216 (TestCanonicalUniqueIDCarriesForcedSensorSuffix) covers only the generic site; neither integration snapshot contains a forced-sensor row, so the MQTT and model identities are not compared anywhere.

stands.title: Two different truth tables decide the same boolean sysvar write
stands.evidence: Quotes verified verbatim. internal/model/hub/sysvar.go:203-208: `case string:` / `switch v {` / `case "true", "True", "TRUE", "1", "on", "ON":` / `return hmtypes.BoolValue(true), nil` / `case "false", "False", "FALSE", "0", "off", "OFF":`. internal/model/hub/sysvar.go:797-803: `case hmtypes.ValueKindString:` / `switch strings.ToLower(v.String) {` / `case "true", "t", "yes", "y", "on", "1":` / `return true, nil` / `case "false", "f", "no", "n", "off", "0":`. Third spelling pkg/hmtypes/support.go:88-92: `case "y", "yes", "t", "true", "on", "1": return true, nil` (unknown strings return false, no error). Liveness: sysvar.go:138 `pv, err := sysvarParamValue(s.Meta().ValueType, raw)` sits inside the `set_value` handler registered at sysvar.go:133; a repo-wide grep for `.Invoke(` outside _test.go (internal/north/matter/im/invoke.go, internal/model/device/update.go:155, custom-DP payload self-calls, internal/central/adapter/mqtt_sink.go:342, custom_dp_dispatcher.go:287) finds no caller that resolves a hub datapoint as a payload.Source. The only Invoke of this service is internal/model/hub/hub_sysvar_param_test.go:73. Every live transport instead builds the ParamValue itself and calls Sysvar.Set -> toWire -> boolToWire: internal/north/rest/handlers/hub.go:1011 `v, err := hmtypes.NewParamValue(req.Value)` then `s.Set(r.Context(), v)`; cmd/openccu-loom/ws_adapters.go:639-643 (WS set_sysvar); internal/central/adapter/mqtt_sink.go:250-253 `pv, err := hmtypes.NewParamValue(value)` / `return sv.Set(ctx, pv)`. hmtypes.NewParamValue (pkg/hmtypes/value.go:119) maps a string straight to StringValue, so the live path always reaches boolToWire's list. hmtypes.ToBool has no caller anywhere in the repo (grep hits only pkg/hmtypes/support_test.go).
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false, sysvar.go:205 would have carried the same token set as :799 or delegated to it/hmtypes.ToBool. It does not: "yes"/"y"/"t"/"no"/"n"/"f" exist only at :799, the case-sensitive spellings "True"/"TRUE"/"OFF" only at :205 - three distinct literal lists in three files. For the liveness half, a production invoker would have shown up as a non-test `.Invoke(` on a hub datapoint or as a hub service-method MQTT subscription; the subscriber list (internal/north/mqtt/command_subscriber.go:501-536) has `/+/hub/sysvars/+/set` -> handleSysvar -> SetSysvar only, with the per-service-method wildcard `"/+/+/+/+/custom/+/set/+"` restricted to channel custom-DPs.
stands.reason: The duplication is real - the same rule (which string means true for a LOGIC/ALARM sysvar) is spelled three times with three different vocabularies, and the service copy feeds the wire copy (double coercion) when invoked. But the candidate's damage story is wrong in its specifics: REST, WS and MQTT do NOT reach sysvarParamValue; all three construct the ParamValue with hmtypes.NewParamValue and land on boolToWire, so no operator can observe a per-transport vocabulary difference today. What is left is a dead-but-live-looking truth table plus a dead public helper; severity is low because nothing regresses when either drifts, and only rises if a hub service dispatcher is ever wired (the precedent for exactly that trap is documented at internal/central/payload.go:66-78).
stands.divergence: LOGIC sysvar, payload "yes": sysvarParamValue returns `%w: %q expects boolean` (payload.ErrServiceInvalidParam); boolToWire returns true. Payload "tRuE": sysvarParamValue rejects (case-sensitive list), boolToWire lowercases and returns true. Payload "maybe": boolToWire errors, hmtypes.ToBool returns (false, nil) - a silent off for an alarm variable.
stands.deadCopy: internal/model/hub/sysvar.go:205 (sysvarParamValue's LOGIC table) - reachable only through the `set_value` service, which no production code invokes; and pkg/hmtypes/support.go:82 (ToBool) - no caller in the repo at all.
stands.guard: TestSysvarToWireLogicAndAlarm (internal/model/hub/sysvar_wire_test.go:28) exercises the toWire/boolToWire side only; internal/model/hub/hub_sysvar_param_test.go:121 exercises sysvarParamValue in isolation. No test compares the two vocabularies, so drift is unguarded.

stands.title: The LIST label-to-index rule is written twice, with different bounding
stands.evidence: Quotes verified. internal/model/hub/sysvar.go:896-900: `case hmtypes.ValueKindString:` / `for i, label := range valueList {` / `if label == v.String {` / `return i, true`; the float branch at :880-895 bounds first - `if v.Float < 0 || v.Float > math.MaxInt32 { return 0, false }`. internal/model/hub/sysvar_subtypes.go:206-217: `switch v := value.(type) {` / `case int:` / `idx = v` / `case float64:` / `idx = int(v)` / `case string:` / `for i, label := range valueList {` / `if label == v {` / `idx = i`, preceded by sysvar_subtypes.go:202-204 `if len(valueList) == 0 { return fmt.Errorf("sysvar %q: no value list configured", ...) }` and followed by :227 `return s.Set(ctx, hmtypes.IntValue(idx))` - i.e. the wrapper resolves the index and then Set resolves it again via toWire (sysvar.go:741-747: `if idx, ok := resolveListIndex(v, m.ValueList); ok { return idx, nil }`, else `return s.intToWire(v)` when the list is empty). Liveness: resolveListIndex is live (sysvar.go:743, on the Set path all three transports use). SysvarDpSelect is constructed only by WrapSysvar (internal/model/hub/sysvar_subtypes.go:320) and a repo-wide grep for `WrapSysvar` / `SysvarDpSelect` / `SendVariable` outside _test.go returns nothing but the definitions and doc comments - the only callers are internal/model/hub/sysvar_program_dp_test.go, sysvar_subtypes_test.go, sysvar_sensor_metric_hub_test.go and sysvar_metadata_race_test.go:88. REST/WS/MQTT all hold a plain *hub.Sysvar (internal/north/rest/handlers/hub.go:1000 `s, ok := h.Sysvar(name)`).
stands.negativeControl: Had the rule been written once, sysvar_subtypes.go:200 would have called resolveListIndex (or just handed the raw value to Set) instead of carrying its own type switch, empty-list rejection and `int(v)` narrowing. Had the wrapper been live, grep would have shown a non-test construction of SysvarDpSelect or a call to WrapSysvar; both greps are empty outside _test.go.
stands.reason: Two independent implementations of 'caller selection -> zero-based LIST index' exist and already disagree on concrete inputs. The pair is asymmetric: the wire copy is live, the wrapper copy has no production caller, so today the disagreement is only visible to tests - which is the worse shape, because the wrapper's tests stay green while the daemon uses the other rule. Severity low on current damage (no operator path reaches SendVariable), but the wrapper is dead code that reads as production API.
stands.divergence: (a) float64 -0.5 on a LIST sysvar with 3 labels: SendVariable computes `int(-0.5)` = 0, passes the `idx < 0 || idx >= len` check and writes index 0; resolveListIndex takes `if v.Float < 0 { return 0, false }` and toWire returns `sysvar %q: value ... not in value list`. (b) LIST sysvar with an empty ValueList and value 2: SendVariable returns `sysvar %q: no value list configured`; the live path (Set -> toWire, sysvar.go:748) falls through to intToWire and writes 2. Case sensitivity does not currently diverge - both compare with `==`.
stands.deadCopy: internal/model/hub/sysvar_subtypes.go:200 (SysvarDpSelect.SendVariable) - SysvarDpSelect is only ever built by WrapSysvar or a struct literal in _test.go files; no production caller of either.
stands.guard: TestSysvarToWireList (internal/model/hub/sysvar_wire_test.go:169) covers resolveListIndex; TestSysvarDpSelectSendVariableByIndex/ByString (internal/model/hub/sysvar_program_dp_test.go:137/160) cover the wrapper. No test compares them.

stands.title: A declared numeric bound is coerced to float64 by two rules that disagree on non-numeric bounds
stands.evidence: Quotes verified. internal/model/hub/sysvar.go:435-450: `func SysvarBoundAsFloat(pv *hmtypes.ParamValue) *float64 {` / `if pv == nil || pv.IsNone() { return nil }` / `case hmtypes.ValueKindFloat:` ... `case hmtypes.ValueKindInt:` ... `default:` / `return nil`, documented at :428-434 as returning nil for 'a non-numeric kind (e.g. a LIST sysvar's spurious bound)'. internal/model/hub/sysvar_subtypes.go:342-350: `func paramValueToFloat64(v hmtypes.ParamValue) float64 {` / `case hmtypes.ValueKindFloat: return v.Float` / `case hmtypes.ValueKindInt: return float64(v.Int)` / `default: return 0`. Its only use is internal/model/hub/sysvar_subtypes.go:153-156: `minVal := paramValueToFloat64(*m.Min)` / `maxVal := paramValueToFloat64(*m.Max)` / `if value < minVal || value > maxVal {`. Liveness: SysvarBoundAsFloat is live in three north planes - internal/north/rest/handlers/hub.go:1058-1059, cmd/openccu-loom/ws_adapters.go:611/614, internal/central/adapter/hub_mqtt_publisher.go:901-902. paramValueToFloat64 is reachable only from SysvarDpNumber.SendVariable, and SysvarDpNumber is constructed only at internal/model/hub/sysvar_subtypes.go:332 inside WrapSysvar, which has no non-test caller (grep for WrapSysvar / SysvarDpNumber outside _test.go returns only the definitions and doc comments).
stands.negativeControl: Had the two agreed, sysvar_subtypes.go:342's `default:` arm would have returned the same 'no bound' signal as sysvar.go's `default: return nil` (or the range check would have called SysvarBoundAsFloat and skipped on nil). It returns the in-band value 0 instead. Had the range check been live, grep would have found a production construction of SysvarDpNumber; it finds none, and the REST/WS/MQTT write paths call *Sysvar.Set directly with no bounds check at all.
stands.reason: The duplication is real: one datum (a declared Min/Max ParamValue) is coerced to float64 by two rules, and the second turns 'absent/non-numeric' into the in-band value 0 - not two right readings for two callers, but a latent [0,0] range. The candidate's damage claim is refuted in its specifics, though: nothing in production builds SysvarDpNumber, so no live write path runs that range check, and an operator cannot see a number entity that refuses every value. Severity low: the defective copy is unreachable today.
stands.divergence: A sysvar whose Min and Max are StringValue("10")/StringValue("30") (or a LIST sysvar's spurious bound): SysvarBoundAsFloat returns nil for both, so the REST summary, the WS descriptor and the MQTT number discovery advertise no bounds; paramValueToFloat64 returns 0.0 for both, so SysvarDpNumber.SendVariable would reject every value except exactly 0 with `sysvar %q: value %v out of range [0, 0]`.
stands.deadCopy: internal/model/hub/sysvar_subtypes.go:342 (paramValueToFloat64) - its sole caller SysvarDpNumber.SendVariable is built only via WrapSysvar or test struct literals; no production caller.
stands.guard: None comparing the two. TestSysvarBoundAsFloat (internal/central/adapter/hub_mqtt_publisher_sysvar_test.go:16) pins the nil-for-non-numeric side; TestSysvarDpNumberSendVariable* (internal/model/hub/sysvar_program_dp_test.go:20-105) pin the 0-for-non-numeric side without ever asserting the non-numeric case.

stands.title: Numeric strings are parsed by two different acceptance rules on the same sysvar write path
stands.evidence: Quotes verified. internal/model/hub/sysvar.go:237-241 (INTEGER, service path): `case string:` / `var n int` / `if _, err := fmt.Sscanf(v, "%d", &n); err == nil {` / `return hmtypes.IntValue(n), nil`; :222-225 (FLOAT): `var f float64` / `if _, err := fmt.Sscanf(v, "%f", &f); err == nil {`. internal/model/hub/sysvar.go:847-849 (intToWire): `if n, err := strconv.ParseInt(v.String, 10, 32); err == nil && n >= math.MinInt32 && n <= math.MaxInt32 {` / `return int(n), nil`; :816 (floatToWire): `if f, err := strconv.ParseFloat(v.String, 64); err == nil {`. Measured the acceptance difference with a throwaway Go program outside the repo (not in the repo, nothing built or tested in-tree): "12abc" -> Sscanf %d n=12 err=<nil>, ParseInt err=invalid syntax; "3.7" -> Sscanf %d n=3 err=<nil>, ParseInt err=invalid syntax; " 7" -> Sscanf %d n=7 err=<nil>, ParseInt err=invalid syntax; "3.7x" -> Sscanf %f f=3.7 err=<nil>, ParseFloat err=invalid syntax. Liveness is the same picture as c001: the Sscanf copy sits in sysvarParamValue (called only from the `set_value` handler at sysvar.go:138, which nothing invokes in production), while REST (internal/north/rest/handlers/hub.go:1011), WS (cmd/openccu-loom/ws_adapters.go:639) and MQTT (internal/central/adapter/mqtt_sink.go:250) all go hmtypes.NewParamValue -> Sysvar.Set -> toWire -> intToWire/floatToWire.
stands.negativeControl: Had the two rules agreed, "12abc" and "3.7" would have produced the same outcome on both sides; the measurement above shows Sscanf accepting both (12 and 3) while strconv rejects both. Had the Sscanf copy been live, a non-test caller of Sysvar.Invoke("set_value") would exist - none does; the only one is internal/model/hub/hub_sysvar_param_test.go:73.
stands.reason: Two acceptance rules for 'is this string a number for an INTEGER/FLOAT sysvar', and the lax one silently truncates. The truncation is a genuine latent defect (an INTEGER sysvar written as 3 for the payload "3.7", no error), and the int32 bounding that makes the narrowing safe on armv7 exists only on the strconv side. But because the Sscanf copy is unreachable from every shipped transport, no operator sees a 422-on-one-transport/silent-truncation-on-another split today; severity low, and the honest fix is to delete the dead handler or route it through toWire.
stands.divergence: INTEGER sysvar, payload "12abc": sysvarParamValue -> IntValue(12) -> Set -> toWire -> intToWire sees ValueKindInt and writes 12; the live REST/WS/MQTT path makes StringValue("12abc") -> intToWire -> `sysvar %q: value 12abc is not an integer`. Payload "3.7" on an INTEGER sysvar: service copy writes 3, live path errors. FLOAT sysvar, payload "3.7x": service copy writes 3.7, live path errors.
stands.deadCopy: internal/model/hub/sysvar.go:224 and :239 (sysvarParamValue's FLOAT/INTEGER string branches) - reachable only through the un-invoked `set_value` service.
stands.guard: TestSysvarToWireInteger (internal/model/hub/sysvar_wire_test.go:108) and TestSysvarToWireFloatAndNumber (:74) cover the strconv side only; hub_sysvar_param_test.go:121 covers sysvarParamValue in isolation. Nothing asserts the two accept the same strings.

stands.title: "What the inbox contains" is stated over three sets in merged() and two in Remove()
stands.evidence: Quotes verified verbatim. internal/model/hub/inbox.go:150-152: `out := make(map[string]InboxDevice, len(i.devices)+len(i.pending)+len(i.awaiting))` / `for addr := range i.awaiting {` / `out[addr] = i.awaiting[addr]`. internal/model/hub/inbox.go:293-301: `i.swap(func() bool {` / `_, known := i.devices[address]` / `_, deferred := i.pending[address]` / `if !known && !deferred {` / `return false` / `}` / `delete(i.devices, address)` / `delete(i.pending, address)` / `return true`. There is no reference to i.awaiting anywhere in Remove (grep -n awaiting internal/model/hub/inbox.go returns 88, 92, 110, 150-152, 174, 185, 192-193 only). Both sites are LIVE: merged() is reached from Count() (inbox.go:115-119) and List() (inbox.go:132-142), which feed the REST payload (internal/north/rest/handlers/hub.go:1089) and the MCP tool (internal/north/mcp/tools_hub.go:364); Remove() has exactly one production caller, internal/central/adapter/device_admin.go:205 `u.HubModel.Inbox.Remove(address)`. The third set is also live: internal/central/adapter/pending_devices.go:78 `u.HubModel.Inbox.SetAwaitingRelease(out)`, called from central_bringup.go:346, device_pipeline.go:664, pending_devices.go:115 and :146. The stale prose that hid the third set is verified too: inbox.go:81 `// Inbox aggregates the "pending device" view an operator has to act on.` / `// It has two sources:`, inbox.go:131 `// List returns the pending devices of both sources, sorted by address.`, inbox.go:114 `// Count is the number of pending devices across both sources.`, inbox.go:287 `// Remove drops a single pending device by address from both sources,` — all written for a two-source world while the struct carries three maps (inbox.go:86-92).
stands.negativeControl: Had the claim been false, Remove would have enumerated the same maps merged() does — i.e. a `_, awaiting := i.awaiting[address]` term plus `delete(i.awaiting, address)` inside the closure at inbox.go:293-301, or merged() would not have walked i.awaiting at 151-152. The grep for `awaiting` in inbox.go would then have shown a hit inside the Remove body; it shows none between line 193 and line 307.
stands.reason: The duplication is real: two methods each restate which per-address sets constitute the inbox, and they already disagree. Severity is low rather than medium because the one reachable production path does not produce a wrong operator view. At device_admin.go:205 Remove is called only after `AcceptInboxDeviceRemote` returned ErrInboxDeviceNotFound with `deferred == false`; for an awaiting-only address Remove returns false, notInInbox is set, and AcceptInboxDevice ends at device_admin.go:239 with `fmt.Errorf("%w: device %s", interfaces.ErrInboxDeviceNotFound, address)` — a 404. The entry surviving is in fact correct there: an awaiting-release device is genuinely still awaiting release, and i.awaiting is derived state rebuilt from ModelRegistry+IsReleased on every PublishAwaitingRelease (pending_devices.go:53-78), so a delete would be reverted by the next sweep anyway. The cost is the maintenance one Q1 asks about: a fourth set, or a change to what counts as inbox content, must be made in two places, and the doc comments that should have carried the rule still describe two sources.
stands.guard: None for the third set. TestInboxRemove (internal/model/hub/inbox_test.go:102-140) populates the inbox only through `in.Replace([]InboxDevice{...})` and never touches SetAwaitingRelease or SetPendingCreation, so it stays green whichever maps Remove deletes from. TestAwaitingReleaseReachesTheInboxSurface (internal/central/adapter/awaiting_release_surface_test.go:22) pins only that a withheld device reaches List(); it never calls Remove.
stands.divergence: Address `DEV_AWAIT1` present only in i.awaiting (i.e. materialised and withheld — the state PublishAwaitingRelease writes at pending_devices.go:78). merged() returns it, so Count() == 1 and List() includes it with AwaitingRelease=true; Remove("DEV_AWAIT1") hits `if !known && !deferred { return false }` (inbox.go:297-298), deletes nothing and returns false, so swap() fires no subscriber. One method says the address is in the inbox, the other says it is not present.
stands.deadCopy: Neither. merged() and Remove() both have production callers (Count/List → REST handlers/hub.go:1089 and MCP tools_hub.go:364; Remove → central/adapter/device_admin.go:205).

stands.title: The index-to-label rendering of a LIST sysvar is written twice — and both copies are dead; the live one is a third
